articles.title: U.S. Strikes Iran in First Military Action in a Month
articles.body:
President Donald Trump vowed on Monday that the U.S. will strike Iran “hard” after the two countries exchanged their first publicly confirmed attacks in weeks.
Trump told Fox News’ Trey Yingst that “there will be a response” to strikes Iran launched against U.S. forces in Jordan overnight in retaliation for an American attack on an island in the Strait of Hormuz.
“We're going to hit them hard,” the President said, according to Yingst.
Trump’s threat comes after U.S. forces attacked two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island on Sunday, marking a resumption of military action after a roughly month-long pause.
CENTCOM spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins confirmed the strike in a statement to TIME, adding that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) forces “were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines” into the strait.
Last week, U.S. forces finished clearing sea mines from the strait’s international shipping routes.
“U.S. forces are monitoring the area closely and remain prepared to protect the free flow of commerce through this essential waterway,” Hawkins added.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) issued a statement soon after the U.S. strikes that was carried by Iranian state news agency IRNA, saying that Iran would respond to the attacks on Larak Island “with punishment for the aggressor.”
The IRGC later said in a statement early Monday local time that it had launched ballistic missiles at a U.S. air base in Jordan and warned that “every shot will be met with more devastating responses,” IRNA reported. Jordan’s armed forces said they intercepted eight missiles that entered the country’s airspace early Monday morning.
In a statement, CENTCOM rebuffed the Revolutionary Guards’ claims, describing the Sunday attack as “limited, precise action against IRGC minelaying forces posing an imminent threat” to the strait.
A pause in attacks
Before the Sunday strikes, the last time the U.S. military confirmed targeting Iran was on July 29, announcing a “heavy wave of strikes” on dozens of IRGC targets in Iran, including command centers, missile and drone facilities, and coastal surveillance and defense sites.
On Aug. 1, President Donald Trump said that he agreed to “hold off” strikes in Iran at the request of the U.S.’s regional allies in the Middle East.
How the U.S.-Iran war began
The strikes mark the latest escalation in the war, which began on Feb. 28 when the U.S. and Israel launched a wave of attacks across Iran. Trump described the operation as a “massive and ongoing” campaign intended to eliminate what he called imminent threats from the Iranian regime and openly encouraged Iranians to overthrow their government.
The attacks came after U.S.-Iranian negotiations over Tehran’s nuclear program failed to produce an agreement and amid the Iranian government’s deadly crackdown on nationwide protests. Trump had accused Iran of rebuilding its nuclear capabilities following U.S. and Israeli strikes on three major Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025. Iran has consistently denied seeking a nuclear weapon.
Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was killed in the opening salvo of the Feb. 28 campaign. Iran retaliated by firing missiles at Israel, U.S. military bases and other sites across the Middle East, widening the conflict throughout the region.
The war also led Iran to militarize and largely close the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy transit routes, through which about a fifth of global oil production typically passed before the hostilities.
A U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports was lifted under a June agreement, but Trump reimposed it after that deal and its accompanying cease-fire fell apart.

articles.title: American nuke sub skips post-shakedown due to availability
articles.body:
The US Navy has declared the Virginia-class attack submarine USS Massachusetts ready for fleet tasking after completing shakedown trials, waiving the boat’s planned post-shakedown availability because of its material condition and combat readiness.
The U.S. Navy announced the decision on 17 August, saying the submarine had completed extensive testing and evaluation following delivery and would move directly into fleet availability rather than entering the maintenance period normally associated with a newly commissioned submarine.
USS Massachusetts, hull number SSN 798, was delivered by Newport News Shipbuilding on 21 November 2025 following sea trials and commissioned in Boston on 28 March 2026.
The Navy said the decision to waive the post-shakedown availability was based on the condition of the submarine during trials and the requirement to make the boat available for operational tasking.
Chief of Naval Operations Admiral Daryl Caudle said in the U.S. Navy release: “USS Massachusetts is ready to fight, and that is exactly where we need her, in the hands of our Sailors and available to the Fleet.”
He added: “Waiving this availability reflects the exceptional condition of the ship and our determination to deliver combat-ready capability faster. It also allows our shipbuilding workforce to focus its talent and capacity where we need it most, building the next generation of submarines our nation requires.”
A post-shakedown availability normally follows the initial period of operations for a new warship or submarine, allowing the Navy and shipbuilder to address defects identified during trials, complete outstanding work and incorporate alterations before the vessel enters routine fleet service. In the case of Massachusetts, the Navy said the submarine met and exceeded the construction and safety standards required during its trials and subsequent shakedown period.
Vice Admiral Rob Gaucher, Director of Submarine Programs, said the decision represented a deliberate departure from the normal process. He said: “Waiving a submarine’s post-shakedown availability is an example of driving efficiency, innovation and speed in shipbuilding.”
Gaucher added: “While it is a calculated risk, we do it without ever compromising the safety of our sailors or the quality of our submarines. By getting this boat into the fight we can continue to maintain an absolute advantage in the undersea domain.”
USS Massachusetts is the seventh Block IV Virginia-class submarine. It was constructed under the long-running teaming arrangement between General Dynamics Electric Boat and HII’s Newport News Shipbuilding. The Block IV boats incorporate design and maintenance changes intended to reduce major maintenance periods over their service lives and increase the amount of time available for deployments compared with earlier members of the class. Virginia-class submarines are nuclear-powered fast attack boats designed for anti-submarine warfare, anti-surface warfare, strike operations, intelligence collection and special operations support.
Vice Admiral Rick Seif, Commander, Submarine Forces, said in the release: “Massachusetts brings unmatched stealth and lethality to the undersea battle force.”He added: “This decision will immediately add combat readiness and capacity to ensure our nation’s ability to dominate and maintain undersea superiority.”
The U.S. Navy’s decision also avoids placing another newly delivered submarine into a shipyard availability at a time when the US submarine industrial base is supporting construction of additional Virginia-class boats alongside Columbia-class ballistic missile submarines and maintenance of the existing fleet.
USS Massachusetts is the fifth US Navy vessel to carry the name and entered service as the latest addition to the Navy’s fast-attack submarine force. With the shakedown period complete and the planned post-shakedown availability waived, the submarine is now available for operational tasking by the fleet.

Ukraine’s supply of Patriot interceptors remains critically constrained as global stocks of the US-made missiles come under pressure. Patriot is one of the few systems available to Ukraine capable of reliably intercepting the ballistic missiles Russia uses in attacks on Ukrainian cities.

articles.title: Ukrainian company builds single device that detects FPV drone, reads its video feed, and jams it
articles.body:
A Ukrainian defense company has built a single device that finds an FPV drone, reads its video feed, and jams it. Rebel Group has developed Brama, a stationary electronic warfare and reconnaissance system to counter FPV drones, which it plans to codify for use by the Defense Forces, the company's press service told Oboronka.
Brama can both detect a drone's signal and jam it, allowing an operator to move from spotting a drone to suppressing it.
Two jobs from one point
Brama can detect the frequency of an analog video signal, decode it, and then apply directed electronic warfare to suppress both the video channel and the drone's control link, the press service explained. Once an operator receives target data and locates a drone, they can suppress it immediately without additional equipment, Militarnyi reports.
"Both functions are implemented in a single device, so the operator does not need to use additional equipment to move from detection to suppression," a Rebel Group representative says.
Rebel Group is seeking codification
Brama has already passed laboratory testing and trials in combat conditions, according to the company. It is now going through Ukraine's military codification procedure, the required step before defense equipment can be approved for broader use by the armed forces.
Its producer company, Rebel Group, specializes in electronic warfare and reconnaissance systems, and some of its equipment has already been codified and tested at the General Staff's proving grounds, the press service noted.
It joins a widening Ukrainian EW effort
Brama is one of several recent Ukrainian counter-drone systems. In July, Ukraine unveiled Lima Quant, an upgraded electronic warfare system built to defeat the advanced satellite-navigation antennas Russia now fits to Shahed drones, cruise and ballistic missiles, and guided bombs, United24 reported.
Those antennas, newer 12- and 16-element arrays, had proven resistant to earlier jammers, which is why each side keeps building the next countermeasure as the other adapts.

DUBAI – Iran is still seeking a negotiated solution to its conflict with the US, President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Aug 31, a day after the two countries resumed hostilities for the first time since late July, driving oil prices up more than 3.5 per cent.
Pezeshkian’s comments also came after US President Donald Trump posted an AI-generated video clip that he said showed Iran’s oil hub Kharg Island being destroyed.
There was no evidence of any such attack, and a US official said on Aug 31 that the military had not targeted Kharg Island in overnight strikes. An Iranian official dismissed Trump’s post as “laughable”.
US forces on Aug 30 struck two Iranian launchers on Iran’s Larak Island, some 660km east of Kharg, a US official said, prompting Iran to strike two US bases in Jordan, according to Iranian media.
Two people were killed, and others were injured in the attack on Larak Island, Iran’s IRNA news agency quoted the local governor as saying on Aug 31.
The return to hostilities followed weeks in which Trump’s administration has stepped up efforts to punish Tehran and its business partners with costly economic sanctions, shifting away from military options. Diplomacy remains in stalemate.
Pezeshkian, speaking to India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of a regional security meeting in Kyrgyzstan, accused the US of failing to fulfil its commitments under past agreements.
“Nevertheless, we are still trying to achieve an agreement and understanding, and we believe that continuing the war is in no one’s interest, neither ours, nor the region’s, nor humanity’s,” Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency quoted him as saying.
“We believe the solution to the existing issues is dialogue and cooperation and that every capacity must be used to prevent the spread of insecurity and conflict.”
‘Blown to smithereens’
Earlier, Trump had annoyed Iran by posting on his Truth Social platform the AI-generated video clip with the message: “Kharg Island being blown to smithereens!!! President DJT.”
Reuters confirmed that the video clip showing dramatic explosions was most likely synthetically generated, using software that detects AI-manipulated imagery.
The White House and the US Defense Department did not respond to Reuters requests for comment outside regular business hours.
Kharg handled 90 per cent of Iran’s oil exports before the US and Israeli launched attacks on Iran on Feb 28, sparking a war that would severely disrupt its energy trade and put huge pressure on the economy.
“Trump’s tweets are laughable, and conditions in Kharg are calm and appropriate,” said Hamid Bovard, chief executive of government-run National Iranian Oil, on Aug 31.
Oil operations had not stopped, and workers were busy repairing previous damage and modernising facilities, Bovard said in comments cited by Nournews, a semi-official outlet close to Iran’s top security body.
Iran vows to respond to any attacks
A US official said forces had attacked the Iranian launchers on Larak Island on Aug 30 after “Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz”.
Larak is a small island in the strait near the strategic Iranian port of Bandar Abbas. The Strait of Hormuz, which normally handles a fifth of global crude oil and liquefied natural gas shipments, has been effectively blocked since the start of the war.
In a statement, the US Central Command said it took “limited, precise” action against minelaying forces of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards that posed an “imminent threat” in the strait. It gave no details.
As well as attacking the US bases in Jordan, Iran’s army said it had also struck the Al Minhad airbase in the United Arab Emirates early on Aug 31. However, the UAE’s defence ministry dismissed that report as false.
The UAE Defence Ministry later said its air force engaged a drone that had come from Iran over its territorial waters. It provided no further details, including whether it was shot down.
The Jordan strikes targeted US bases used to launch and support the attack on Larak, Iran’s Foreign Ministry said.
The Revolutionary Guards used air defence missiles to shoot down a US drone that crashed in Gulf waters, the Mehr news agency said on Aug 31, citing a statement from the elite force.
A supertanker caught fire and was brought to a complete halt after being struck by two naval mines in the southern Strait of Hormuz, Iran state TV said, citing a Guards’ statement.
Piling economic pressure on Iran
Trump has yet to achieve the objectives he set out at the start of the war: dismantling Iran’s nuclear programme, curbing its ability to attack regional rivals and creating conditions for Iranians to overthrow their clerical rulers.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Reuters on Aug 30 new secondary sanctions were likely to be unveiled weekly in the effort to pressure Iran, with an initial focus on banks.
The European Union said on Aug 31 it would continue to work with the US and others to maintain economic pressure on Iran.
The Guards said the supertanker on fire after being hit by mines had been attempting to pass through the waterway illegally, but gave no details of the vessel or crew, according to a statement cited by state television.
Last week, Trump said all mines had been detonated or removed from the international waters of the strait and Iran had been warned that any vessel placing new mines would be destroyed.
Iran denied Trump’s assertion. REUTERS

articles.title: Is Russia’s fuel crisis a temporary squeeze or the collapse of an industry? Two leading economists debated the question, unable to agree on how much refining capacity is left.
articles.body:
Is Russia’s fuel crisis a temporary squeeze or the collapse of an industry? Two leading economists debated the question, unable to agree on how much refining capacity is left.
On August 17, Sergey Vakulenko, a senior fellow at the Berlin-based Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, said on The Breakfast Show that despite Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries, Russia’s refining output remains fairly high. By his estimate, refining has fallen by only 25–28%. Two days later, economic commentator Vyacheslav Shiryaev criticized Vakulenko on the same program, calling his remarks “nonsense.” He said 65–70% of Russia’s oil refining has been knocked out, and that any optimistic assessment only helps prolong the war. After trading criticism at a distance, the two agreed to debate — first in writing, then in person on The Breakfast Show. Here’s what came of it.
In the first two sections, Meduza recaps the written portion of the debate, which the independent Russian outlet Novaya Gazeta Europe has already published. The third covers the closing stretch of the in-person discussion, when the participants answered questions from the host. (In the debate’s first part, the two sides repeated the questions and answers Novaya Gazeta had already published.) Meduza has preserved the meaning of every statement, though parts of the debate may have been edited or rearranged. Some questions and answers have been left out.
Sergey Vakulenko answers his opponent’s questions
What share of Russia’s production capacity for marketable gasoline and diesel fuel remains at this point?
Our understanding of Russian oil refining lags behind events, so it’s hard to say precisely how things stand today. For gasoline, the July 2026 range is 2.25 million to 2.65 million tons a month, compared with 3.5 million tons in March 2026. For diesel, the July 2026 range is 5.2–5.6 million tons, compared with 7.7 million tons in March 2026. The share of production capacity devoted to gasoline and diesel tells you nothing useful. Plants are very rarely run at full capacity. Exact output figures for specific products are classified. If Russia were producing 27% of its April 2026 gasoline output, as you claim, the fuel wouldn’t be reaching ordinary Russians at all. Your claim that damaged units can’t be replaced is incorrect: most of them are made in Russia.
You said this August’s crisis isn’t very different from the gasoline crises before 2022 and in 2023. By what criteria was that comparison made?
I never said the current crisis is much like the ones of previous years. What I meant was that the old problems — the ones bad laws and seasonal demand spikes cause almost every year — have been compounded by new ones caused by the strikes on refineries.
Do you agree with the data from Izvestia showing that fuel is available at only 28% of gas stations? If those figures are correct, why do you say there’s no crisis?
I said that the situation is serious and that refining volumes have fallen noticeably. But different people mean different things by the word “crisis.” I prefer quantitative assessments to qualitative labels. I studied Izvestia’s figure, and it’s misleading. You can arrive at it arithmetically, but it doesn’t mean what people usually understand by the phrase “fuel was available at 28.1% of gas stations nationwide.” GdeBENZ, a service that shows which stations have fuel, is fine for finding a station that might have gasoline, but you can’t draw sweeping conclusions from its data.
Vyacheslav Shiryaev answers his opponent’s questions
What primary data do you base your assessments on, for individual plants and for the country as a whole?
Official data on fuel output aren’t available, and what Russia’s state statistics service, Rosstat, publishes is a lie. For several months now I’ve been keeping a running spreadsheet on 40 refineries. I build it from official statements about plant shutdowns, data from analytics firms, reports in industry Telegram channels, information from sources in Russia’s energy sector, and messages from subscribers sent through an anonymous Telegram bot. I can share that spreadsheet with you.
Since the end of May, you’ve been saying that Russia’s oil refining is running at 30–35% of March levels. Where does that number come from, why hasn’t it changed, and why don’t you rely on data from Rystad, Bloomberg, and Kpler, which give higher estimates?
At the end of May, I was talking about the remaining volume of marketable gasoline production, not the overall volume of oil refining. The brief stabilization in the fuel market had two causes: Ukraine, for a time, shifted to destroying warehouses belonging to the retailer Wildberries, and the Russian government introduced anti-crisis measures. Western analytics firms can’t be trusted here, since they rely on official data from the Russian authorities. I’ll believe Bloomberg when someone points me to the person who can heroically and systematically leak information to “enemy” media without clearing it with Russia’s presidential administration — and never get caught.
What effect do you expect from your catastrophic forecasts? Do you consider yourself an expert or a fighter in the information war?
In all my forecasts, I specify that they hold only if Ukraine maintains the same intensity of strikes as in the previous week, or in whatever week. Ukraine has its own ideas about the strategy for destroying refineries. I’m the only public expert to have predicted the June fuel crisis, and I did so on May 20. If another expert says something true that I don’t like, I won’t argue. But repeating the Kremlin’s talking points about a “strong economy” and “no problems with gasoline” is unacceptable. They mislead Ukraine’s top leadership, prolong the war, and play into the aggressor’s hands.
Experts answer the host’s questions
If so little gasoline is being produced, as you say, why are cars still on the road?
Vyacheslav Shiryaev: Drivers spend more time waiting in line than driving. If gasoline is available at 28% of gas stations, you spend your time in line instead of on the road. Everything happening at gas stations confirms my numbers. If Ukraine keeps striking refineries as regularly as it has lately, only a handful of people will still be driving. Everyone else will fall back on public transportation, which isn’t built to handle that kind of load.
Do you think Russia’s oil refining industry is resilient enough that drone attacks can’t do it serious damage?
Sergey Vakulenko: A year ago, I wrote that at the level of drone pressure Ukraine was applying then, Ukraine couldn’t inflict irreparable damage. If it widens its reach, strikes more often, and delivers more explosives per raid, these plants could be destroyed sooner or later. But as of 2025, I wasn’t seeing that. I can see a scenario in which the plants really do start coming apart, but that moment hasn’t arrived yet.
Why are Russian refineries being hit at all, and why are they so poorly defended?
Vyacheslav Shiryaev: At first, no one knew how to defend them; then we saw how ineffective the defenses were. There are too many refineries, and they’re scattered across Russia. There’s no system of defenses built up over five years, the way there is in Ukraine.
Sergey Vakulenko: The short answer is that drones are so cheap and so numerous that modern military doctrine has no response to them and sees no effective defense. Even at a 95% interception rate, if 10 drones get through, they’ll do damage.
What’s the current balance between destruction and repair? Are Ukraine’s armed forces destroying plants faster than the plants can be rebuilt, or the other way around?
Sergey Vakulenko: What does “now” even mean? Ust-Luga came under heavy attack in April, and for as long as the strikes were daily, the port there sat idle. As soon as the strikes stopped, it went back to work. The same goes for refineries. If you send a swarm of 200 drones against a plant every 10 days, you can keep it offline indefinitely. After that, it’s a question of budget and of how many drones Ukraine’s armed forces have.
Vyacheslav Shiryaev: The plant in Orsk won’t run for six months — that’s an official statement from the governor. It’s a similar story at one of Lukoil’s biggest plants. You don’t need to keep the plants under constant pressure; you just need to finish “taking out” the remaining units. That’s the fundamental difference from a port: there’s nothing at a port you can “take out” to paralyze the whole operation.
Could refineries be placed under temporary state management under Putin’s new decree, on the grounds that they’re poorly protected critical infrastructure?
Sergey Vakulenko: They could! I haven’t asked lawyers what the decree means, but there’s no point poring over the decrees Russia is issuing now. It will be whatever they want it to be.
Vyacheslav Shiryaev: If I were Lukoil, I’d be worried — the company is first in line. Four plants are down, and I wouldn’t be surprised if Lukoil gets carved up.
Where will Ukraine’s campaign of strikes lead, and when will Russia run out of gasoline?
Vyacheslav Shiryaev: Gasoline will never run out completely. There are refineries drones can’t reach. Some fuel will always come in from Belarus, unless it decides to enter the war. At some point, Russia will be down to producing 10,000–15,000 tons of gasoline a day. If Ukraine finishes off the remaining plants, Russia is doomed.
Sergey Vakulenko: I disagree with Vyacheslav on the numbers, but Ukraine’s armed forces really do have the physical capacity to stop gasoline production in the European part of Russia. In the Asian part, it’s harder.
Will 92-octane gasoline cost 200 rubles a liter? And if so, when?
Vyacheslav Shiryaev: If they decide at Ukraine’s presidential offices on Bankova Street in Kyiv that gasoline will cost 200 rubles in two weeks, then that’s what it will cost. It’s all in Ukraine’s hands. They don’t even need more drones; they just need to finish off what’s left.
Sergey Vakulenko: There are plenty of reasons the price could hit 200 rubles. The state could decide that it no longer needs to subsidize gasoline consumption — that it will let “the market sort it out.” Then gasoline would cost 200 rubles, but without the lines. The other scenario is intensified attacks, leaving the government no choice but to raise the price. It’s a real possibility, but I won’t try to predict when.

articles.title: Kremlin Says Putin Sees ‘Absolutely No Point’ in Trump-Zelensky Peace Summit
articles.body:
The Kremlin on Monday poured cold water on the prospect of a three-way peace summit between Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, saying there is “absolutely no point” in such a meeting without a deal ready to be signed.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said any meeting between the three leaders would only make sense if it were held to formally seal agreements ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“You know the position of our head of state well: such a meeting is possible only to fix agreements,” Peskov said, adding that a settlement would be a “very complex process” involving numerous details.
He also accused Kyiv of refusing to pursue what Moscow calls a “real settlement” of the war.
Peskov’s comments came after reports that CIA Director John Ratcliffe proposed a trilateral summit during a secret Aug. 25 visit to Moscow.
Sources cited by Axios reported that Ratcliffe raised the possibility of bringing Trump, Putin and Zelensky together.
Trump first floated the idea of a trilateral summit in August 2025, saying preparations were underway and suggesting it could happen within two weeks. More than a year later, the meeting has yet to take place.
According to The Wall Street Journal, Trump personally sent Ratcliffe to Moscow without informing some of his closest aides and military commanders beforehand.
Ukraine and Israel Draw Closer as Israeli Elections Loom
During the visit, Ratcliffe met with Russia’s top security officials, including SVR chief Sergei Naryshkin and FSB Director Alexander Bortnikov.
Axios sources said the CIA director sought to determine whether Russia’s security chiefs could persuade Putin to return to negotiations.
The New York Times reported that Ratcliffe delivered Bortnikov a “bleak assessment” of the Russian military and economy and urged Moscow to strike a deal before its position deteriorated further.
Yet the Kremlin’s latest message suggests Putin remains far from ready to compromise.
After Ratcliffe’s visit, Ukrainian Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov said US-mediated talks between Ukrainian and Russian delegations could take place in September.
Kyiv, however, remains skeptical of Moscow’s intentions.
Budanov’s deputy, Pavlo Palisa, said Putin had ordered Russia’s military to prepare several scenarios for an offensive in northern Ukraine, including possible advances toward Kyiv and Chernihiv.
Meanwhile, the Kremlin continues to demand that Ukraine surrender the remaining Ukrainian-held parts of Donbas, where Kyiv’s forces control roughly 20% of the territory.

articles.title: Taiwan defense ministry vows cost-efficient military modernization
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The defense ministry on Monday pledged to maintain efficient defense procurement that maximizes value and controls costs while ensuring military readiness.
In a report, the ministry listed the weapons and systems it plans to purchase to strengthen national defense, per CNA.
The ministry plans to procure portable counter-drone systems and new combat and armored vehicles. Funds will also be allocated to upgrades of the Navy’s Hai Lung-class submarines and underwater trials for the Narwhal submarine, according to CNA. The Navy will build a submarine rescue vessel and a replenishment ship, as well as buy more attack drones and unmanned surface vehicles, the ministry said.
The ministry said it will procure Strong Bow interceptors designed to counter tactical ballistic missiles, along with other missile systems, to build a layered T-Dome air defense network, CNA reported. It will also establish a digitized communications network to support decentralized command.
Regarding US arms purchases, Taiwan will acquire M109A7 self-propelled howitzers, HIMARS rocket systems, Switchblade 300 systems, and ALTIUS 600ISR and ALTIUS 700M loitering munitions.
As new equipment is gradually introduced, the military will phase out outdated systems that no longer meet future operational requirements, the ministry said, per CNA. Equipment and organizational structures in reserve forces will be reviewed and adjusted based on operational scenarios and mobilization readiness.
The ministry said China uses coast guard ships, maritime militia, legal warfare tactics, and economic coercion to tighten control over the Taiwan Strait and increase pressure on Taiwan.

articles.title: US Trains Polish Special Forces to Operate in High-Drone-Activity Zones, Drawing on Ukraine War Experience
articles.body:
In Germany, Polish special forces are taking part in military exercises designed to teach them how to operate in areas where they could easily be detected by drones.
The Associated Press reports that the U.S. military developed the training program based on lessons learned from the war in Ukraine.
The special forces are practicing how to move through a 3,000-square-kilometer area controlled by a simulated enemy and how to carry out simulated strikes on key targets using drones.
According to the exercise scenario, the Polish troops must secretly move through the positions of U.S. soldiers playing the role of the enemy.
The U.S. troops also monitor reports from local residents to the police, which could help them detect and locate the Polish team.
The special forces must then travel about 100 kilometers across Germany to reach another training area in Grafenwöhr, where they are tasked with destroying a simulated target.
During the mission, the troops must avoid detection not only by military personnel but also by civilians. To do so, they move through villages and farms, where surveillance cameras are also in operation.
The U.S. military plans to conduct these exercises several times a year and expects special forces from more NATO countries to take part.
Meanwhile, the U.S. approach to developing counter-drone capabilities remains unclear.
Shortly before these exercises, the U.S. Army shut down a specialized unit in Europe that focused on studying warfare involving drones.
Despite this, the United States has been systematically studying the use of drones in Russia’s war against Ukraine for several years.
This work is carried out both by specialized units and by combat formations, which receive new drones and counter-drone systems to test during military exercises.
One of the key initiatives is the Transforming in Contact (TiC) program, under which the U.S. Army delivers new technologies directly to combat units for testing during deployments and training.
The 3rd Brigade Combat Team, 10th Mountain Division tested new drones, electronic warfare systems, command-and-control systems, and mobile platforms while deployed in Europe.
The brigade fielded more than 150 unmanned systems of various types, designed for a range of different missions.
Another initiative is the JIATF 401, a U.S. military interagency task force responsible for countering unmanned aircraft systems. Its main mission is to rapidly integrate advanced counter-drone technologies into military units.
JIATF 401 personnel are also studying the experience of Ukraine and European countries, where the widespread use of drones has become a routine part of modern warfare.

articles.title: US trains Polish special forces using lessons from Ukraine's war against Russia – AP
articles.body:
US trains Polish special forces using lessons from Ukraine's war against Russia – AP
US forces have begun training Polish special forces in Germany using exercises designed to "simulate many of the challenges" of Russia's war against Ukraine.
Source: Associated Press
Details: Polish special forces are taking part in exercises designed only a few months ago which simulate breaking through enemy lines, travelling for miles through hostile territory and using drones to strike a key enemy target.
Associated Press noted that the exercises, initially developed by US Army Green Berets for American special operations units, began on Friday 28 August and incorporate and simulate many of the challenges faced by Ukrainian forces in the war against Russia.
"We're using lessons learned from Ukraine," a US Army Green Beret officer attached to the training facility said. "All of those effects that we're seeing either Russia or Ukraine having to overcome – we're doing our best to replicate."
The exercises highlight efforts by some US military units to study the latest methods of drone warfare, which Ukraine has pioneered during more than four years of fighting to repel the full-scale invasion launched by Russia. They also demonstrate how the US, its NATO allies and Ukraine are working together to prepare for the possibility of further Russian aggression in the coming years, even as US President Donald Trump's administration has warned of troop reductions in Europe.
During the exercises in Germany, a senior soldier told AP that similar training is planned to take place several times a year.
A participant and officer involved in the exercises told AP that they expect most, if not all, NATO countries to be interested in sending troops to take part.
The exercise scenario lasts several days and takes place across a vast 3,000-square-kilometre training area in the Bavarian countryside.
The Polish special forces are expected to sneak past a US Army airborne infantry unit whose soldiers will play the role of the enemy. The US airborne unit will parachute into a restricted training area at the Hohenfels base and establish itself on the line of contact.
If the Polish troops manage to get past the US forces, they must head north, travelling about 100 km through the German countryside to another training area in Grafenwöhr, where they are expected to destroy a simulated target.
German farms and villages, private and government-operated cameras and a densely populated town lie along the route. These not only create obstacles but also increase the likelihood of the Polish troops being spotted.
A senior serviceman told AP that during earlier stages of the exercises, the Green Berets removed their uniforms "so they can blend in", adding that "blend in also means don't get seen by civilians".
AP added that local German civilians are largely unaware of the exercises and provide a useful test of how effectively special forces can blend into the local population. If they fail, reports of suspicious individuals made to the police will be passed to the military, which will use them to pinpoint the group's location.
The US Army will also use its own drones to search for the Polish units.
If they are detected, "now you have the entire Russian arsenal coming at you", a US soldier said.
The US Army could either send a military police unit with dogs to search for the Polish special forces or deploy additional drones to the area. In previous versions of the exercise, the US Army had more than 100 drones at its disposal, the soldier said.
As part of the exercises, servicemen may be "captured or killed".
AP noted that while the exercises demonstrate the use of drones and NATO teamwork, there have recently been differing views within military circles about the importance of cooperation and the value of drones.
Trump has caused confusion among NATO allies by repeatedly changing his position on possible reductions in the number of US troops stationed in Europe, while his administration has begun a review of US military forces to determine its next steps. Last week, the US Army's top military commander also disbanded a unit specialising in drone warfare.
Quote from AP: "But overall, there is growing interest in tapping Ukraine for its expertise on modern warfare and, specifically, drones."
Details: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in March that Ukraine was helping five countries in the Middle East and the Persian Gulf counter Iranian drone attacks carried out during the US war against Iran. Those seeking assistance included both the US and European countries.
Meanwhile, the number of mysterious drone incursions across Europe has increased, including this month, when two drones were spotted over a German military base and a drone carrying explosives was discovered at one of Germany's key cargo airports.
Background:
- During the Combined Resolve exercise in Germany, Ukrainian drone operators from the Nemesis unit – the 412th Brigade of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces – quickly detected and simulated strikes on vehicles belonging to a US mechanised brigade, demonstrating their superiority in the use of drones.
- The Combined Resolve exercise in Germany, held in April and May, showed that the US troops from Texas taking part were unprepared for the capabilities of Ukrainian drone operators.

articles.title: Ukraine and Israel Draw Closer as Israeli Elections Loom
articles.body:
Relations between Ukraine and Israel appear to be entering a period of cautious rapprochement, with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reaching out directly to President Volodymyr Zelensky as Israel approaches national elections.
In a letter marking Ukraine’s Independence Day on Aug. 24, Netanyahu congratulated Zelensky and the Ukrainian people, praised Ukraine’s resilience, and described Iran as a common threat facing both countries.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Zelensky made the letter public two days later, saying Ukraine and Israel share deep ties between their societies, economies, and cultures.
“It is therefore good to hear of Israel’s desire to strengthen these existing ties,” Zelensky wrote. He added that Kyiv was counting on productive cooperation to increase security.
Netanyahu also added a handwritten note referring to his brief meeting with Zelensky in Washington in late July.
The Washington meeting
The two leaders spoke and shook hands at the funeral of the late US Sen. Lindsey Graham on July 28, during Zelensky’s visit to Washington. It was their first face-to-face contact since September 2023 and their first reported conversation since January 2025.
Attempts to arrange a formal bilateral meeting in Washington did not produce one, but the brief exchange was described as cordial.
The same day, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar spoke with Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha and invited him to visit Israel. Sa’ar identified Iran as a threat facing both countries and said he wanted to deepen cooperation with Ukraine.
Can Ukraine Set a New Standard in International Law?
The contacts marked a noticeable change after several years of complicated relations between Kyiv and Jerusalem.
Stolen grain strained relations
Israel has provided Ukraine with humanitarian aid, advanced early-warning technology, generators, and components for Patriot systems since Russia launched its full-scale invasion. It has nevertheless resisted Kyiv’s requests for major Israeli weapons systems and maintained channels with Moscow.
Relations then deteriorated sharply in April over grain shipments to Haifa that Kyiv said originated in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories.
Ukraine first called on Israel to investigate after the Russian vessel Abinsk arrived in Haifa carrying wheat allegedly taken from occupied Ukraine. Kyiv later asked Israeli authorities to arrest the shipment, but the vessel left and the cargo was never detained.
The dispute escalated when a second vessel, the Panormitis, approached Haifa with another cargo allegedly linked to occupied Ukrainian territory. Kyiv summoned then Israeli Ambassador Michael Brodsky and prepared an official protest note.
Sa’ar dismissed Kyiv’s public criticism as “Twitter diplomacy,” arguing that Israel had not received a formal request to seize the vessel or detain the cargo. The Israeli foreign ministry later said Ukraine’s legal-assistance request contained factual gaps and lacked supporting evidence.
The Israeli importer ultimately rejected the Panormitis cargo, but the public dispute exposed broader tensions over Israeli military assistance, Ukraine’s voting record at the UN, and the way the two governments communicated.
Iran creates common ground
The US-Israeli war against Iran has created significantly more common ground between Kyiv and Jerusalem.
Iranian-made Shahed drones have been used extensively by Russia against Ukraine, giving Kyiv years of experience in intercepting the weapons that are also central to Israel’s security concerns.
In March, Kyiv Post reported that Jerusalem had approached Ukraine about possible cooperation against Iranian drones. A source in Zelensky’s office said Ukraine was open to working with Israel and could share operational experience and domestically produced drones. Kyiv, in return, expected greater Israeli military support.
Ukraine has since expanded its role in the Middle East by offering its drone-interception experience to regional partners while developing relations with Israel and the Gulf states.
Israel has remained sensitive to Ukraine’s contacts with regional governments that have difficult relations with Jerusalem. These tensions were among the issues in a July Kyiv Post analysis of what the Iran war means for Ukraine.
Elections
The current improvement in relations is unlikely to produce an immediate major change in Israeli policy toward Ukraine, despite support for closer cooperation in some Israeli political and security circles.
Israel will hold national elections on Oct. 27. The president will then consult the parties elected to the Knesset and assign a member of parliament to form a government.
Under Israeli law, that person initially receives 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible extension of up to 14 days. The process could therefore continue into December, and longer if the first nominee fails.
A Kyiv Post source in Jerusalem said they do not expect major decisions concerning Ukraine before the election and the formation of the next Israeli government.
According to the source, the largest window for significantly expanding Israeli assistance to Ukraine opened roughly two years ago. No comparable shift should be expected during the current election period.
For now, the rapprochement is therefore more likely to produce renewed political dialogue and work on specific areas of common interest than an immediate change in military assistance.
The election will determine whether Netanyahu remains in office or a new coalition takes power. Kyiv is already positioning itself to work with the government that emerges.

articles.title: Cornered by Stalemate, Putin Prepares to Escalate the War in Ukraine
articles.body:
- Category

Cornered by Stalemate, Putin Prepares to Escalate the War in Ukraine
Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s refusal to back down in Ukraine is rooted in the survival instincts of Russia’s “gangster politics,” The Economist reported on August 30.
The report noted that the cornered leader is now planning to escalate the war against Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
His predatory worldview was recently on display during an August 29 meeting with university students in Moscow, where Putin bizarrely claimed that orcas eat polar bears to illustrate “the food chain” and justify the war.
While factually inaccurate, The Economist noted that the remark provided a window into the mindset of a leader facing a strategic dead-end. With the Russian army stalemated and suffering tens of thousands of casualties each month, and Ukrainian drone strikes inflicting visible damage on Russian infrastructure, Putin is seeking a new way to escalate his way out of the crisis.
Western intelligence agencies are increasingly anxious about his next moves. The Economist highlighted several recent indicators of this growing alarm: CIA Director John Ratcliffe unexpectedly flew to Moscow on August 25, Finland requested Swedish military assistance to monitor its border for incursions, Romania destroyed a Russian naval drone targeting a drilling platform, and authorities in Germany and Slovakia foiled suspected sabotage plots linked to Moscow.
Putin himself has ended his long silence regarding Ukraine’s successful drone campaign against Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs, including warehouses belonging to the e-commerce giant Wildberries. In an August 22 address, he accused Ukraine of opening a “Pandora’s box” and promised severe retaliation.
Earlier that same day, he dismissed any notion of peace negotiations, vowing to his political party that the military operation would move “only forward.”
Sources close to the Kremlin told The Economist that after weeks of deliberation over the summer, Putin appears to have formally chosen the path of escalation. Waning public tolerance for the war is becoming an increasing concern; independent polling from the Levada Centre shows 57% of Russians now describe the situation as “tense,” citing the rising death toll, mobilization fears, and a lack of a future.
The mood among the Russian elite is even more pessimistic. Insiders cited by The Economist reveal a growing consensus that the nearly five-year war is a failure because of the sheer amount of time wasted, regardless of the outcome. However, the criminal logic guiding Putin’s regime dictates that he can never show weakness.
A failure to achieve even his minimum goal of capturing the entire Donbas region could put his life in physical danger. “They will hang me,” he reportedly confessed to cronies earlier in the war, The Economist wrote.
While the exact shape of the impending escalation remains unclear, The Economist suggests Russia will likely intensify hybrid warfare and sabotage operations targeting European supply routes to Ukraine. On the battlefield, Russian sources indicate Putin is prepared to throw an additional 300,000 to 400,000 men into the fight.
Rather than announcing a highly unpopular new mobilization wave, the Kremlin is expected to rely on localized coercion by regional governments to fill the ranks. Ultimately, these escalatory measures are designed to project strength and ensure regime survival, even as they guarantee further instability and suffering.
Russia’s manpower crisis is further underscored by Western intelligence estimates indicating Moscow is losing roughly 6,000 more troops each month than it can recruit. Despite enlisting about 1,000 personnel daily, the Kremlin remains unable to cover battlefield casualties, driving Russian forces to intensify long-range missile strikes against Ukraine’s civilians instead.

articles.title: Poland Joins US Drone-Warfare Drills Built on Ukraine’s Battlefield Lessons
articles.body:
Polish special forces are taking part in US-led drills focused on drone warfare as Poland seeks to bolster its capabilities in the event of a potential confrontation with Moscow.
The multiday exercises, which began Friday, are taking place at the Joint Multinational Readiness Center near the town of Hohenfels in southern Germany, the US Army’s main combat training center in Europe.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The exercise was initially developed for the Green Berets, the US Army’s special forces and was designed around Ukraine’s battlefield experience in its war with Russia.
This is the first time a NATO ally such as Poland has taken part in the training.
During the drills, Polish forces will operate under a scenario in which they must covertly bypass enemy positions, travel about 100 kilometers through German countryside controlled by a simulated adversary, and use a drone to strike an important target, according to an exclusive report by The Associated Press (AP).
The reported route runs from Hohenfels toward the Grafenwöhr Training Area, a major US Army and NATO training site near the town of Grafenwöhr in Bavaria, southern Germany.
‘Lessons’ from Ukraine
According to the report, the exercise is planned to take place several times a year and may eventually include military personnel from most or all 32 NATO countries.
“We’re using lessons learned from Ukraine,” a US special forces officer told AP.
Kremlin Says Putin Sees ‘Absolutely No Point’ in Trump-Zelensky Peace Summit
“All of those effects that we’re seeing either Russia or Ukraine having to overcome — we’re doing our best to replicate,” he added.
The drills come amid heightened concerns about a potential confrontation between Russia and NATO countries, as well as questions about the level of US commitment to the alliance.
Last week, CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow on a surprise visit. Multiple media outlets reported that the trip was intended in part to warn Russia against attacking NATO countries. US President Donald Trump, however, said Ratcliffe had not been sent to deliver a specific warning.
Meanwhile, reports of unexplained drone incursions across Europe have increased. Earlier this month, two drones were spotted over a German military base and a drone carrying explosives was found at a key German cargo airport.

articles.title: Trump threatens retaliation against Iran, calls for leaders to face war crimes trial
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has threatened a military response to Iranian attacks on US forces in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, while calling for Iran’s leadership to face trial over his allegations that it killed more than 100,000 protesters.
“We’re going to hit them hard. There will be a response,” Trump told Fox News on Monday, after Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said it had launched ballistic missiles at the King Hussein and Azraq airbases in Jordan and explosive drones at Al Minhad Air Base in the UAE.
The IRGC said the strikes were retaliation for a US attack on Larak Island on Sunday that reportedly targeted efforts to place sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global oil shipments.
Trump said US air defence systems intercepted most of the incoming attacks. He added that one missile was allowed to pass after being assessed as unlikely to hit anything significant.
Trump escalates pressure on Tehran
Separately, Trump called Iran’s leadership “officially a failed nation” and accused its authorities of killing protesters on a massive scale.
“They must be tried for war crimes against humanity,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, alleging that more than 100,000 demonstrators had been killed.
The reported death toll has not been independently confirmed.
Trump also claimed Iran had been severely weakened, saying it had “no Navy,” “no Air Force” and “no currency,” while describing its leadership as being in “total disarray.”
His remarks add to mounting tensions as Washington and Tehran remain at odds over the conflict, sanctions and the Strait of Hormuz.
Diplomacy remains uncertain
Trump said Tehran was seeking a meeting but expressed skepticism about an imminent diplomatic breakthrough, arguing that US sanctions were now “kicking in strongly.”
The latest exchange of threats comes as military confrontation and economic pressure continue to overshadow diplomatic efforts to ease the conflict.

articles.title: Russia shows off new laser weapon against drones
articles.body:
- A Russian military blogger published footage claiming a Russian laser weapon system has destroyed several hundred Ukrainian drones near strategic sites in southwestern Russia.
- The claims, including a planned second-generation system for intercepting aircraft and cruise missiles, have not been independently verified.
Footage circulating in Russian pro-military channels this week shows what is claimed to be a Russian laser weapon system engaging aerial drones, according to a Russian military blogger who described the video as an “exclusive.”
The blogger’s post claimed several such systems are now protecting strategic sites in southwestern Russia and that the laser complexes have destroyed several hundred Ukrainian drones. The claim has not been independently verified, and no Russian government or military agency has confirmed the figures.
“Only we have sensational footage of the destruction of Ukrainian drones in the sky by a combat Russian laser complex,” the blogger wrote. “Several of these laser installations now cover our strategic facilities in the southwest of the country.”
Based on the footage, the system appears to be a containerized platform combining a laser weapon, a targeting and guidance system, and a command post where an operator controls the unit. The system reportedly includes its own detection setup for tracking aerial threats, combining radar and visual sensors, according to the footage.
The blogger’s post also claimed developers are preparing a second-generation version of the system, intended to intercept faster targets, including tactical aircraft and cruise missiles.
“I am not inclined to overestimate this innovative type of weapon based on ‘new physical principles,’ but combined with traditional air defense systems, a combat laser will definitely be useful for protecting the country from air raids,” the blogger wrote. “It is also gratifying that we not only have such combat ‘purple beams,’ but they have also proven their effectiveness. Now these ‘Jedi swords’ need to be developed and constantly improved. Such is the path.”
Directed energy weapons for counter-drone use have drawn increasing interest from multiple militaries in recent years, though publicly verified operational combat use against drone swarms remains limited across all countries developing the technology. Laser weapons face documented limitations including reduced effectiveness in poor weather, atmospheric interference over longer ranges, and thermal management requirements for sustained operation.
The claims made in the Russian footage, including the number of drones destroyed, the specific location of the systems, and the timeline for a second-generation variant, have not been corroborated by independent sources or confirmed by official Russian military statements.

articles.title: Russia plans to control drones from two-seater Su-57D fighter jet
articles.body:
Russia plans to control drones from two-seater Su-57D fighter jet
Russia has outlined the tasks for which it plans to use the two-seater variant of the Su-57D fighter jet, a prototype of which is currently undergoing flight tests.
Source: Russian state corporation Rostec
Details: Russia claims that the aircraft made its first flight in May 2026.
Rostec has identified two main tasks for the new modification. The first involves using the aircraft for training to practise special flight modes which, the company claims, cannot be replicated on ground-based simulators.
The second task involves testing technologies that Russia classifies as sixth-generation. The developers intend the second cockpit to enable the Su-57D to serve as an airborne control station for unmanned systems.
Mikhail Strelets, Director of the Sukhoi Design Bureau, said this capability is important for controlling the S-70 Okhotnik drone, as well as drone swarms and groups, when the main pilot's attention is focused on carrying out the primary combat mission.
In addition, representatives of Russia's United Aircraft Corporation said that the two-seater Su-57D is planned to be used to test so-called combat artificial intelligence technologies that the corporation's specialists are currently developing.
However, Russia has not provided any test results confirming the Su-57D's claimed capabilities for controlling drones or employing artificial intelligence technologies.
According to Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU), the S-70 Okhotnik ("Hunter") is a Russian reconnaissance and strike UAV. Its stated maximum take-off weight is 25 tonnes, its range is 6,000 km, and its maximum speed is 1,400 km/h.
Background: Previously, DIU revealed details of a new Russian cruise missile developed for the Su-57 fighter jet.

articles.title: Poland intercepts Russian spy plane over Baltic Sea again
articles.body:
- Polish fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft over the Baltic Sea on Monday, 30 kilometers north of Łeba.
- Poland's defense minister said the aircraft did not violate Polish airspace, in at least the third such intercept reported this year.
Polish fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft over the Baltic Sea on Monday, roughly 30 kilometers (19 miles) north of Łeba on Poland’s coast, Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said.
“Russia has once again tested our deterrence and air defense systems,” Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote. “Before noon, 30 km north of Łeba, our fighters intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft. There was no violation of our airspace over the Baltic.”
The aircraft did not violate Polish airspace, according to the minister. Monday’s intercept was at least the third publicly reported Il-20 intercept by Polish fighters over the Baltic Sea this year, following similar incidents in March, May and July.
The Il-20, known by NATO as the “Coot-A,” is a Soviet-designed signals and electronic reconnaissance aircraft derived from the Il-18 airliner. Russia regularly flies the aircraft over the Baltic Sea to collect electronic and communications intelligence, and the flights have become a recurring trigger for NATO quick reaction alert sorties in the region.
In several previous intercepts this year, Polish officials said the Il-20 was operating without a filed flight plan and with its transponder switched off. In March, Poland’s Operational Command of the Armed Forces said one such intercept marked the aircraft’s ninth reconnaissance mission of the year in the region, describing the pattern as a sustained Russian intelligence-gathering effort rather than an isolated event.
Poland has used both MiG-29 and F-16 fighters to carry out Il-20 intercepts over the Baltic this year. The MiG-29, a Soviet-designed aircraft, remains in a shrinking quick reaction alert role as Poland phases in newer F-16 and FA-50 fighters, with some retired Polish MiG-29s transferred to Ukraine.
Kosiniak-Kamysz has previously described the Il-20 flights as deliberate provocations intended to test Polish and NATO air defense response times, radar coverage and command-and-control coordination along the alliance’s eastern flank.

articles.title: US forces strike two Iranian launchers on Iran’s Larak Island, US official says
articles.body:
US strikes Iranian launchers in first action in a month, triggering retaliation
Tehran targets American bases in Jordan; UAE intercepts drone as regional tensions spike again
US forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz in their first military action in a month on Sunday, breaking a lull in fighting during an intermittent war that has lasted more than six months. Vowing to retaliate for what it called a deadly attack, Iran later said it had launched missiles at US sites in Jordan.
Forces with the Revolutionary Guard Corps were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait, according to Tim Hawkins, a spokesman for the US Central Command (CENTCOM). The US military last week completed clearing sea mines from the strait’s international shipping routes.
Semi-official news outlets in Iran reported sounds of explosions near Larak island on the strait. The Guard in a statement carried by Iran’s state broadcaster noted “the martyrdom and injury of several of our fighters and compatriots”.
Later, Iranian state television showed what it said were ballistic missiles being fired by Iran at US bases in Jordan in response to the American strikes. Jordan’s armed forces said they intercepted eight missiles that penetrated the country’s airspace early Monday in the Middle East.
The UAE Defence Ministry said its air force intercepted an Iranian drone over territorial waters and dismissed claims by Tehran that Dubai’s Al Minhad Air Base was targeted.
US military officials disputed Iran’s claim that the latest American strikes were an act of aggression, calling them a “limited, precise action” against what they said were minelaying forces.

articles.body:

Ukraine Knocks Out Two Russian Pantsir-S1 Air Defense Systems in Back-to-Back Strikes
Ukrainian forces destroyed two Russian Pantsir-S1 short-range air defense systems in separate strikes in temporarily occupied Crimea and Russia’s Krasnodar region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The first Pantsir-S1 was destroyed near the temporarily occupied city of Kerch on August 29, while the second was hit a day later near a military airfield in Yeysk, Krasnodar region, according to the open-source channel Dossier Shpiona, which published images showing the destroyed systems.
OSINT project CyberBoroshno reported that Russian forces had positioned a decoy near the Pantsir-S1 in Yeysk. The presence of the decoy did not prevent the operational system from being identified and struck.
The Pantsir-S1 is a Russian self-propelled short-range surface-to-air missile and anti-aircraft artillery system designed to protect military and other critical facilities against aircraft, cruise missiles, and drones.
The system combines two twin-barrel 30 mm 2A38M automatic cannons with up to 12 surface-to-air missiles. Its cannons can engage targets at ranges of up to approximately 4 kilometers (2.5 miles), while its missiles can reach targets at distances of up to 20 kilometers (12.4 miles) and altitudes of up to 15 kilometers (9.3 miles).
Earlier, Ukrainian forces struck multiple Russian military targets, including a radar station and an S-400 command vehicle in the Bryansk region, a communications hub in Belgorod, a drone command post near Huliaipole, and logistics depots in temporarily occupied Crimea, Luhansk region, and Russia’s Kursk region, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on August 31.

FT: Musk is ready to allow Ukraine to use Starlink for strikes on the Russian Federation, but the decision must be made by the White House
Kyiv • UNN
Elon Musk has allegedly agreed to Ukraine's use of Starlink-equipped drones against targets in Russia. The final decision must be made by the White House.
Elon Musk is allegedly ready to allow Ukraine to use Starlink-equipped drones to strike Russian targets outside Ukraine. At the same time, the final decision must be made by the White House. This is reported by the Financial Times, according to UNN.
Details
According to the FT, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy approached Elon Musk with a request to allow drones equipped with Starlink to be used against Russian ballistic missile launchers located up to 200 km from the Ukrainian border.
"People familiar with the matter said that Musk had previously told (former Defense Minister Mykhailo — ed.) However, according to sources, Musk told Ukraine that this was a political decision and had to be made by the White House," the publication writes.
For Ukraine, such an opportunity could become a fundamentally new tool in the fight against ballistic missiles. In that case, Ukraine would not wait for a Russian missile to be launched in order to intercept it in the air, but would locate and strike the launchers themselves on the territory of the Russian Federation.
Denys Shtilerman, co-founder and chief designer of the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, previously explained that integrating Starlink into long-range strike systems would make it possible to operate much more effectively specifically against mobile targets in the Russian rear.
"Instead of shooting down arrows, we will strike the archers," Shtilerman explained the logic behind this approach.

Drone factory supplying Ukraine catches fire in Poland: unknown individual spotted on premises
A fire broke out overnight at a factory belonging to WB Electronics in Poland, a company that produces drones for the Ukrainian and Polish armies, among others. Shortly before the fire started, surveillance cameras reportedly captured an unknown individual wearing a balaclava on the company's premises.
Source: Onet, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The incident occurred at the WB Electronics factory in the town of Skarżysko-Kamienna, halfway between Warsaw and Kraków, which produces military drones for the Polish and Ukrainian armies, as well as flight controllers.
The fire broke out on the night of 30-31 August, 23 minutes after midnight. Simultaneously, the operator of the security firm tasked with monitoring the facility alerted police after sensors were triggered, potentially indicating the intrusion of unauthorised individuals.
Surveillance cameras reportedly captured an unknown individual wearing a balaclava who entered the company's premises over a fence. An abandoned rucksack and a long-sleeved top were subsequently found near the factory.
The Internal Security Agency and military counterintelligence were notified of the incident, and police have opened an investigation.
The fire service said the fire was relatively small and was extinguished within two hours. Internal Security Agency officers then arrived at the scene.
"In the case of fires like this, the special services do what they are supposed to do. We take this situation very seriously… We caution against the temptation to spread any disinformation about this. Internal Security Agency officers are working meticulously to determine whether there are grounds to speak of sabotage," said Jacek Dobrzyński, spokesperson for the minister-coordinator for special services.

articles.title: Ukrainians turn anger on Kiev for storing explosives near their homes
articles.body:
Ukrainians turn anger on Kiev for storing explosives near their homes
Residents of the Kiev suburb of Milaya have accused Ukrainian officials of placing an ammunition depot dangerously close to civilian homes, according to interviews published by The Guardian on Monday.
The military storage site was hit last week during a Russian barrage. The Russian Defense Ministry said the attack targeted a warehouse complex storing components for Ukrainian long-range kamikaze drones used in strikes on logistics and e-commerce facilities in Russia.
Secondary explosions continued for hours after the strike, scattering stored military ordnance around homes just hundreds of meters from the depot, local residents told the British newspaper.
“Those who set up the depot here are to blame. There are people here, this is a village. You can’t keep something like that here,” Vera, 65, reportedly said.
She and her son Sergey spent hours sheltering in a small bunker beside their home as dozens of secondary explosions rocked the area.
“I thought it was humanitarian aid that was stored there,” Sergey told the newspaper.
The incident killed at least 38 people and damaged more than 200 private homes and 14 apartment buildings, the Kiev military administration said on Sunday. Thirty of those killed were residents of a care home located close to the ammunition depot, according to The Guardian.
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky said an investigation had been launched into the “terrible negligence” that allowed munitions to be stored so close to civilians.
“Another such crime – after what happened in Vishnevoe – is absolutely unacceptable,” he wrote on X on Saturday.
A Russian strike on an ammunition depot in the Kiev suburb of Vishnevoe on July 6 also triggered massive secondary explosions, damaging hundreds of civilian buildings and causing civilian casualties. Following that incident, Zelensky and other senior Ukrainian officials vowed to prevent munitions from being stored near residential areas.
Storing ammunition near civilian housing could contravene international humanitarian law. Under Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, parties to a conflict must, “to the maximum extent feasible,” avoid locating military objectives within or near densely populated areas.

articles.title: Taiwan military aligns more closely with US combat practices
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The US is increasingly influencing Taiwan’s combat tactics and equipment, according to a Business Insider report.
Chieh Chung (揭仲), a senior analyst at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, told Business Insider that Taiwan is following more US recommendations on training, target identification and strikes, and special forces operations.
"This makes it necessary for the US side to observe live exercises to assess the effectiveness and shortcomings of its recommendations and of bilateral military exchanges, providing a basis for subsequent adjustments and revisions," Chieh said.
This year’s Han Kuang exercises introduced the “backbrief” for the first time, per Business Insider. It is a US military practice in which junior commanders relay their understanding of a mission and its orders to their superiors.
Taiwan is now adopting it as part of efforts to train and authorize lower-level commanders to make their own decisions if communication with superiors is lost.
Lin Ping-yu (林秉宥), New Taipei City councilor and former Taiwanese special forces paratrooper, said, "This highlights an area where Taiwan's military culture urgently needs to evolve," according to Business Insider.
"The traditional mindset of 'mission accomplished at all costs' is ill-suited to modern battlefields," he added.
When asked about US military presence during the Han Kuang exercise, a US State Department spokesperson told Business Insider that the US remains committed to its “one China” policy and to maintaining peace in the Taiwan Strait.
The spokesperson did not confirm if there are military personnel on the ground. However, they said the US helps provide Taiwan with the necessary arms and related support to defend itself.
Some of those weapons were featured during the Han Kuang exercise, including Patriot missiles, M1A2 Abrams tanks, F-16Vs, and High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems, according to Business Insider. Taiwanese troops were also seen launching Anduril’s Altius 600M loitering munitions during drills.
Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey said in June that he hopes to expand manufacturing in Taiwan.
Earlier this month, Taiwan Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) said that Taiwan-US military cooperation “is far closer than you might imagine,” per a Wall Street Journal report. “The public sees only the arms sales, but in fact, it’s multifaceted and involves so much more,” he said.
“Through military exchanges, we have been learning so much practical combat experience from the US,” Koo said. However, the defense minister stressed that Taiwan’s plan for a potential cross-strait conflict does not rely on US military intervention, WSJ reported.

articles.title: Ukraine seeks more drones and air defence from Latvia
articles.body:
Ukraine has asked Latvia to support the rapid delivery of air defence equipment, unmanned ground vehicles, fibre-optic-controlled drones and additional strike capabilities as Kyiv sets out its current battlefield priorities, according to Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence.
Ukrainian Defence Minister Evgeniy Khmara and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces Mykhailo Drapatyi discussed the requirements during a meeting with Latvian Defence Minister Raivis Melnis, the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence announced on 29 August.
The Ukrainian side identified four areas as priorities: unmanned ground vehicles, fibre-optic-controlled drones, what the ministry described as “middle-strike capabilities”, and air defence assets. Khmara also stressed the need for equipment identified as urgent to reach Ukrainian forces as quickly as possible, making delivery times part of the discussions alongside the type of equipment being sought.
Fibre-optic-controlled drones have taken on a growing battlefield role because the control link is carried through a physical fibre rather than relying on a conventional radio connection. The approach can allow operators to retain control in environments where radio-frequency links are heavily disrupted, although the systems bring their own operational limitations.
Unmanned ground vehicles have similarly been employed for an expanding range of battlefield tasks, including logistics and other activities in areas where exposing personnel carries additional risk. Ukraine has increasingly sought to expand the use of uncrewed systems across land, air and maritime operations.
Air defence remains another continuing requirement for Kyiv as Russian forces employ combinations of missiles and uncrewed attack aircraft against targets across Ukraine. The Ukrainian ministry did not identify particular air defence systems being requested from Latvia in its account of the meeting.
Latvia, meanwhile, intends to continue providing security assistance to Ukraine worth at least 0.25% of its gross domestic product each year. Kyiv said it is also looking to Riga to work with other governments and through multinational initiatives to generate further military assistance. The two defence delegations discussed areas beyond the immediate supply of equipment, including rehabilitation for Ukrainian military personnel, training and the development of cyber capabilities.
Ukraine also offered to share operational experience with Latvia. According to the ministry, this could include lessons from multi-domain operations, territorial defence and the construction and development of modern fortifications.
Latvia has been among the NATO members providing sustained military assistance to Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.

articles.title: U.S. Army Command Warns Hegseth Against Expanding Operations Against Iran
articles.body:
U.S. military leadership is warning Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth against further expanding military operations against Iran.
The Washington Post reports that in a recent classified assessment, U.S. military officials warned that a prolonged large-scale operation in the Middle East could weaken U.S. military capabilities in other regions of the world.
These warnings to Hegseth came from the leaders of the U.S. Army, Navy, and Air Force, as well as four-star commanders responsible for U.S. operations in Europe, Asia, and Latin America. They are contained in the August 14 edition of the Secretary of Defense’s Orders Book (SDOB).
The SDOB is typically published twice a month. The document contains information on the global readiness of U.S. ships, aircraft, personnel, and weapons systems.
The compilation reflects the president’s priorities for the armed forces, as implemented by the secretary of defense, and also includes assessments from senior generals and admirals. Based on these assessments, the Pentagon develops further directives.
According to the document, some U.S. forces deployed to the Middle East are expected to remain in the region through the end of September, while other units will remain through 2027. According to sources familiar with the document, the possibility of further extending the deployment is a cause for concern.
The heads of U.S. European Command, U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, and U.S. Southern Command, as well as the Chief of Naval Operations, oppose such plans.
To support operations in the vicinity of Iran, U.S. geographic combatant commands have been forced to redeploy their ships, aircraft, and other equipment to the region.
This is already limiting the U.S. military’s ability to carry out its missions in other regions and maintain the necessary level of combat readiness.
As previously reported, the Pentagon is preparing at least four options for potentially reducing the U.S. military presence in Europe.
However, European officials remain skeptical about the review and suggest that a decision to reduce the U.S. military presence in Europe may have already been made.
