articles.title: Ukrainian Influencer Infiltrates Russian Zoom Meeting Covering Drones, Insults Attendees
articles.body:
A popular Ukrainian prankster hacked a video conference for Russian officials discussing chronic problems in national drone production and ended the meeting by demanding that attendees explain why they were so unprofessional and seemingly intent on stealing government money, according to a recording of the Zoom meeting made public on Sunday.
The breach by Evhen Volnov (handle: “Major Chernobaev”) targeted a virtual meeting attended by representatives of the Russian Federation’s Ministry of Industry and Trade and the Russian state air industry agency Rosaviatsia.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Zoom footage published by Volnov showed 14 Russian officials signed in, including, among others, Rosaviatsia Deputy Head Andrey Potemkin, Evgenia Gvozditsina of the Aviation Register of Russia, and Evgeny Sivaev, deputy director of the drone division at the company Radar MMS.
The Zoom description said the meeting would discuss “the process of certifying developed models of unmanned aviation by organizations and manufacturers.”
Potempkin as chair of the proceedings said that Russian drone manufacturers were underperforming in developing new models of aircraft for his agency’s certification. “We can say that we have room to improve,” Potempkin said, comparing relatively quick Chinese certification of new drones with relatively slow Russian state certification of similar aircraft.
‘They Will Hang Me’: Putin Fears Defeat in Ukraine, Plans to Send 400,000 More Russians to War
Using indirect, bureaucratic language, typical for mid-level Russian officials speaking about an unpleasant fact, he said: “Therefore we must organize our work more responsibly than our colleagues from the Chinese People’s Republic.”
The officials attending the video conference seemed passive. While none interrupted Potempkin’s presentation, most had their video feeds turned off.
Drones have become a war-critical weapon system for Russia, accounting for at least half of all Ukrainian casualties and military equipment losses inflicted by Russian forces. Despite having an economy more than ten times larger than Ukraine’s, Russia likely produces 20-50% fewer military drones by volume. In terms of technology, Ukrainian drone manufacturers have maintained a strong, and at times decisive, advantage over their Russian counterparts since Russia’s first invasion of Ukraine in 2014.
The Ukrainian prankster Volnov hijacked the meeting after Potempkin finished reading off statistics about the relative rates of Russian and Chinese certification of newly-developed drones and opened the floor for discussion.
“Yes, colleagues, there is this question, how is it that Ukrainian engineers assemble effective, combat-capable unmanned air vehicles (UAVs) in the space of three weeks, in primitive conditions, yet Russian aviation, with everyone here sitting at this meeting, billions of rubles spent, and all we have is a little packet of certification documents to show their bosses?”The Russian officials at the meeting did not immediately respond to Volnov’s comments, which under Russia’s wartime laws are not only punishable by more than a decade in prison for the person making them, but can also be incriminating for anyone who intentionally listens to or repeats them.
“How is that on the one hand the enemy (Ukraine) is fighting a war, and meanwhile at the same time you are just siphoning off money from the state budget?” Volnov said.The video showed attendees sitting silently in response to the question. After a brief pause, Potempkin demanded that Volnov identify himself.
“I am Truntek. But can you explain yourself? I mean, I’m sitting here, and all I hear is ‘bla, bla, bla, bla, bla, bla.’”
At the 1:06 mark one attendee uses profanity and another accuses Volnov of being a “provocateur.”
“In my passport it’s written that I’m from the SBU,” Volnov responded, falsely identifying himself as an operator for Ukraine’s national spy agency.
“Thank you for the information. Everything has been recorded. All you participants are recorded. Thank you for the incriminating evidence. And thank you for the interesting and optimistic information.”
Then the video organizer cuts off the conference feed.
Volnov’s commentary accompanying the video said that the meeting had been called to address the fact that Russian drone manufacturers are unable to assemble or certify a single drone unless Beijing supplies the components.
The embarrassing-for-Moscow breach of an official Zoom conference discussing poor drone-certification rates came in the wake of another intrusion publicized by Volkov on Aug. 6. In that incident, he gained access to a closed video conference organized by the Russian Ministry of Defense to discuss the production of anti-drone jamming systems. Representatives of major military contractors, including VoenTorg, VoenTelecom, and OboronLogistics, attended the Zoom meeting, which included at least 25 logins and more than 60 Russian officials.
A cascade of PowerPoint presentations by multiple attendees appeared to show agencies working hard despite limited resources, while arguing that shortcomings in military production were beyond their control. In the video edited by Volnov, balalaika music played in the background and presenters’ remarks were sped up for comedic effect.Volnov disrupted what had until then been a dull, slide-heavy discussion. He pointed out that, despite the efforts of Russian manufacturers of anti-drone jamming systems, thousands of Ukrainian drone strikes continued to hit energy and other critical infrastructure targets across Russia. He then posed a direct question: “Is there any money in the budget for jamming systems at all?”
At least three conference rooms full of attendees were shown picking up papers and walking off-camera, rather than staying and answering Volnov’s question.
“You are all co-conspirators with the regime and you will be held responsible for its crimes. It doesn’t matter what your job is. You know what you are doing and you know that on your hands is the blood of innocent people. Children and women.” Volnov told officials leaving the conference.
In April, per the independent Russian news agency Meduza, Ukrainian operators infiltrated a closed video conference held by Russian army recruiters at Kuban State Agrarian University to drum up volunteers. Volnov on Apr. 4 published a video of an unidentified man calling himself a Ukrainian agent telling potential recruits sitting in a classroom with Russian officers not to sign up.
“I’m actually a serviceman – just not Russian, but Ukrainian. And I want to tell you: God forbid you come here, because I’ll have to kill you – every single one of you who signs that contract. All your faces have been noted.”
Organizers said the break-in was a provocation and cut off the digital feed. Ukrainian news platforms reported about the conference in detail while Russian state media ignored it.

(NOTE TO READER: In Ukrainian “трутень/truten” has the meaning “drone” carrying meanings similar to English, i.e. “male bee,” “lazy person,” and “remote-controlled aircraft.” Kyiv Post AI research found a possible link between “Truntek” and a west Ukrainian dialect term meaning “fool” or “stupid person,” but could not confirm it. The word doesn’t exist in Russian.)

articles.title: US weighs limited strikes on Iran to curb missile, radar rebuild in Hormuz: Report
articles.body:
Merve Aydogan
31 August 2026•Update: 31 August 2026
 The US is weighing limited military strikes in the Strait of Hormuz to stop Iran from rebuilding radar and missile systems used to threaten shipping, Axios reported Monday.
Citing three American officials, Axios reported that US Central Command drafted the plan over the past week and that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth backed it.
The plan had not received presidential approval before this weekend's exchange of fire with Iran, but officials said that could change following the latest escalation, according to the report.
One official said the objective was to reduce the risk of Iranian attacks on oil tankers, US Navy ships and Air Force aircraft, describing the approach as an effort "to mow the lawn."
"The President retains all options at his disposal. The Iranians want to make a deal, but they are always a day late and a dollar short," a White House official told Axios.
Officials cited a recent incident in which an Iranian anti-aircraft missile was fired toward a US F-35 escorting ships in the strait as raising concerns over Iran's military capacity.
They said Sunday's Iranian missile attacks on US bases in Jordan, following a US strike on Iranian troops, could affect Trump's decision.
Trump, meanwhile, told Fox News that the US would "hit them hard" in response.

articles.title: Russia attacks Kyiv for another night as explosions, fires hit Ukraine's capital
articles.body:
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Russia continued its attacks on Kyiv for another night as air defenses in Ukraine's capital shot down Russian drones late into Aug. 31, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
Earlier on Aug. 31, Kyiv faced its fifth day in a row of nonstop Russian jet-powered drone attacks, while Russian strikes in other regions killed at least seven people and injured another 45 over the past day, authorities said.
As nightfall began, Ukraine's air defenses were engaged in Kyiv's city center once again, and several Russian drones were downed over the city, reporters said.
Fires were recorded throughout the city as Russia's attack on Kyiv continued, Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said at 9:30 p.m. local time.
A blaze broke out in the city's Darnytskyi district as a result of a downed drone, in the Solomyanskyi district a wooded area caught fire, and in the Holosiivskyi district drone debris was found at two different locations.
A "very loud" explosion then rocked Kyiv's city center at around 10:17 p.m., Kyiv Independent Deputy Chief Editor Toma Istomina said.
The Kyiv City Military Administration cleared the air raid alert later at 10:27 p.m. local time after it began hours earlier at 7:46 p.m.
In recent days, Kyiv has recorded a record number of air raid alerts as Russia shifts its strategy to launching jet-powered drones in near-hourly attacks rather than its usual massive overnight barrages of ballistic and cruise missiles preceded by waves of drones.
On Aug. 28, the capital recorded 13 alerts, the highest number since Russia launched its full-scale invasion against Ukraine.

articles.title: Russia used five times as many jet-powered drones in July as in June
articles.body:
Russia used five times as many jet-powered drones in July as in June
A Ukrainian military official has said Russia used five times as many jet-powered drones to attack Ukraine in July as it did in June, following a change in its drone attack tactics and increased use of jet-powered UAVs, which are more difficult for the Ukrainian Air Force to shoot down.
Source: Yurii Ihnat, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, in an interview on the national joint 24/7 newscast
Quote: "The enemy has changed the weapons it uses more than its tactics. In other words, it has significantly increased the number of jet-powered [drones – ed.] specifically. This happened... in July. The enemy used five times as many jet-powered UAVs in July as in June. That was the month when the number of these UAVs, along with Banderol missile drones, began to increase significantly."
Details: Ihnat reported that Russia had launched more than 1,500 UAVs on Ukraine over the past four days. Of these, 800 – more than half – were jet-powered.
Ihnat said the Russians have resorted to using jet-powered drones as Ukraine's defence forces were successfully shooting down and jamming large numbers of conventional petrol-powered Shaheds.
"Of course, they did not start using jet-powered UAVs just recently, but they have now increased their use, realising that they cannot be shot down using the conventional methods we already employ against ordinary UAVs," the spokesperson said.
He added that Ukraine's interception rate for jet-powered UAVs is currently lower than for conventional drones, 88-90% of which are shot down.
Ihnat explained that the successful interception of jet-powered drones requires the use of ground-based air defence systems, aviation systems and platforms, fighter jets equipped with air-to-air missiles, and other weapons.

articles.title: "It is a moment of extreme urgency": US senator urges House to approve Russia sanctions bill
articles.body:
"It is a moment of extreme urgency": US senator urges House to approve Russia sanctions bill
US Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut has urged the House of Representatives to support a Senate-passed bill imposing sanctions on Russia, describing the situation in the war in Ukraine as a "moment of extreme urgency".
Source: Blumenthal in an interview with CBS News
Quote: "It is a moment of extreme urgency, for the reason that Putin may try to escalate, but also because Putin is on his heels economically.
And this kind of sanctions bill, throttling the flow of revenue to his war machine could undercut completely his ability to wage this brutal, murderous war."
Details: The US Senate passed the bill by a wide bipartisan majority before breaking for its August recess. The initiative emerged after the sudden death of Senator Lindsey Graham, who had long advocated the measures alongside Blumenthal. The bill has now moved to the House of Representatives, which is due to return to work this week after a five-week recess. However, its prospects in the lower chamber remain uncertain.
The bill, known as the The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, would allow the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest importers of Russian oil or natural gas, except for countries that import less than 15% of their natural gas from Russia while also taking steps to reduce those imports. Some Democrats in the House, however, have raised concerns about giving the president additional powers.
Asked about possible opposition from Democrats, Blumenthal defended the bill, saying it was the "result of painstaking, sometimes painful, negotiations" with the US Trade Representative, the White House and lawmakers from both parties.
"It passed the Senate 86 to 11 – not many measures doing that kind of successful passage these days," Blumenthal said.
He highlighted the additional powers the bill would give the president to "impose scorching sanctions on the oligarchs" and financial institutions, as well as measures to "crack down on the shadow fleet" and the power to impose tariffs, "narrowly constrained" to the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas.
Blumenthal said the sanctions bill could weaken Russian leader Vladimir Putin's position.
Quote: "His economy is on the verge of major crisis.
He has a deficit looming of US$125 billion, 5% of his GDP, an interest rate of 14% on his national debt."
Details: Blumenthal expressed great hope that the sanctions bill would receive enough support from Democrats to pass the House. He added that during his visit to Ukraine last week, he urged President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to meet with members of Congress, as the Ukrainian leader had done in the Senate.
Previously: Zelenskyy met with US senators from both parties – Richard Blumenthal and James Lankford – in Kyiv on 23 August.
Read also: This time could be different for Russia sanctions
Background: The US imposed sanctions on a number of entities within the Russian Defence Ministry as well as two Russian companies and five Russian nationals at the beginning of August.

Why Japan’s hypersonic and underwater weapon plans might worry China

articles.title: "Italy ‘recruits’ Fedorov" — Italy’s top media outlets ran headlines about the former defense minister beginning work for another country
articles.body:
"Italy ‘recruits’ Fedorov" — Italy’s top media outlets ran headlines about the former defense minister beginning work for another country
Kyiv • UNN
Mykhailo Fedorov will advise Italy’s defense minister pro bono on drones and air defense. In Ukraine, there are concerns about a leak of military technologies.
Italian media published articles with headlines stating that Italy is “recruiting” former Ukrainian Minister Mykhailo Fedorov. The articles appeared after Fedorov announced that he had become an adviser to Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto on defence issues, UNN reports.
According to Italian media reports, Fedorov decided to cooperate with Italy, providing it with his expertise.
“It is no coincidence that the main topics of his meeting with Minister Guido Crosetto were drones, air defence and so-called “unmanned” systems—remotely controlled or autonomous vehicles or devices,” Italy’s leading news agency ANSA writes.
The agency reports that, announcing his new position, Fedorov specified that “Ukraine’s experience could become the foundation for a new European defence model”.
“We must be “able to quickly test and implement new solutions, combining technology with reliable production capabilities. Minister Crosetto expressed his satisfaction: I am glad that Mykhailo Fedorov agreed to offer me his services,” ANSA quotes Italy’s Defence Minister.
Fedorov, for his part, stressed that “Ukraine and our team “have experience that we are ready to share”.
“In this position, I will help Italy implement modern technologies of warfare, strengthen its defence sector and adapt to new global security challenges,” Italy’s national news agency Adnkronos quotes Fedorov as saying.
The influential British publication the Financial Times, for its part, writes that Ukrainian MPs, veterans and civil society leaders, including many who supported Fedorov after his dismissal, were outraged by the news of his trip abroad.
“Many questioned his motives when, on Friday, after a visit to Rome, he announced that he would work as an unpaid adviser to Italy’s defence minister. Oleksii Honcharenko, an opposition MP who chairs the parliamentary investigative committee, wrote that Fedorov’s role in Italy could pose “a threat of leakage of knowledge about our advanced military technologies”, the Financial Times wrote.
As is known, the Law of Ukraine “On State Secrets” establishes a special procedure for transferring classified information to a foreign state or international organisation—on the basis of an international treaty or another state decision provided for by law. Such actions carried out privately are illegal.

articles.title: Russia’s Putin and China’s Xi to Attend Summit in Kyrgyzstan
articles.body:
Russia’s Vladimir Putin, China’s Xi Jinping and more than a dozen other leaders will gather in Kyrgyzstan Monday for a two-day summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, a regional bloc that seeks to be a counterinfluence to the West.
The group, which is celebrating its 25-year anniversary, brings together Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Iran, four Central Asian countries and Moscow-allied Belarus.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Arriving in Bishkek on Sunday, Xi hailed what he described as a “golden period” in relations with Central Asian Kyrgyzstan, as China deepens its influence in the historically Russia-dominated region.
Putin and Xi have previously used SCO summits to promote their vision of a multipolar world and present a united front against the West.
It takes place four-and-a-half years into Moscow’s Ukraine invasion and six months into the war between Washington and Tehran. Iran will be represented by its president, Masoud Pezeshkian.
Putin, Xi, Pezeshkian as well as India’s Narendra Modi and Pakistan’s Shehbaz Sharif are due to take part in a plenary session chaired by Kyrgyz leader Sadyr Japarov.
Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdogan is also expected to attend, though his country is not a formal member.
Putin is also expected to hold separate bilateral talks with Iran’s Pezeshkian and China’s Xi, among other leaders, Kremlin spokesman Yuri Ushakov said.
How Russia’s Cultural Projects Conceal Their Human Atrocities
Russia and Iran – among the most sanctioned states in the world – have massively deepened their military and economic ties since Moscow invaded Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump has warned Moscow and Beijing against arming Iran.
Putin’s meeting with Pezeshkian comes days after the CIA’s director John Ratcliffe made a rare trip to Moscow, with US media speculating he could have discussed Ukraine and Iran with his Russian counterparts.
The SCO has historically focused on economic issues, but has gained momentum in recent years under Moscow’s and Beijing’s leadership.
On top of its 10 members, it now has 15 “dialogue partners”, including Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Qatar. It also has two observer countries: Afghanistan and Mongolia.
The SCO’s founding declaration says the group is “not an alliance directed against other states”.
But Putin and Xi have repeatedly made anti-Western speeches during its summits.
At last year’s gathering, Putin accused Western countries of provoking the Ukraine war, while Xi denounced “acts of intimidation”, referring to US-Chinese tensions.
- Real and trade wars -
The Bishkek summit takes place as some SCO members are in the midst of real wars – the Ukraine and Iran conflicts – or trade wars, with the imposition of US tariffs on Chinese and Indian goods.
This month, the US slapped secondary sanctions on Iran’s trading partners in the sectors of gold, technology, digital assets, aviation and maritime transport, aiming to cripple Tehran’s economy.
Washington has also threatened Iran’s allies with sanctions.
China, a major importer of Iranian oil, responded by saying it will “firmly defend” its interests.
Iran, living under sanctions since its 1979 revolution ended with Islamic authorities taking charge, has regularly said it will not cave to economic pressure.
But Pezeshkian has acknowledged his country faces “economic difficulties”.
Iran only joined the bloc in 2023.
Mohammad Hassan Najmi, an international relations expert, told AFP that Tehran “believes its membership and active participation in these alliances can enable it to circumvent US and European sanctions”.
But concrete benefits of the group are uncertain, he said, as “in times of crisis, these alliances have rarely allowed Iran to resolve its difficulties”.
While the bloc claims to represent some 40 percent of the world’s population and 25 percent of global GDP, it remains diverse, with some disagreements among members.
Russia and China compete for influence in Central Asia – a resource-rich region crucial for the transport of goods between Europe and Asia – while Beijing at times has had strained relations with India and Pakistan.

articles.title: Children for the state: Why the Kremlin's demographic policy is fueling social conflict
articles.body:
Children for the state: Why the Kremlin's demographic policy is fueling social conflict
The Kremlin promises financial incentives for having children, expands benefits for large families, and demonstratively "cares" about pregnant students and schoolgirls. The amounts involved are enormous: by 2030, the national "Family" project is set to spend an amount comparable to two years of Ukraine's state budget expenditures. This money is intended for measures that are supposed to encourage higher birth rates — from subsidized mortgages for young families to propaganda promoting large families.
But there is a problem. Our monitoring of two of Russia's most popular social networks — Telegram and VKontakte — conducted in early 2026 shows that absurd legislative initiatives and intrusive demographic propaganda are openly irritating the Russian population. The policy that the Russian authorities call "family support" is becoming yet another source of conflict between the state and society.
If Russia wants to wage aggressive wars in the future, it needs people above all. That is why it is critically important for us to understand how successful the Kremlin is in implementing its demographic programs.
More than two-thirds of the world's population lives in countries where birth rates are below replacement level. Population decline has been a problem for Ukraine since independence, but it became catastrophic after the full-scale war and the mass migration it triggered. Today, Ukraine's total fertility rate has fallen below one.
Our enemy is in a better position, but the situation is far from simple. In 2024, 1.22 million children were born in Russia, one of the lowest figures in its modern history, while the total fertility rate stood at 1.4 children per woman at the end of 2025. It is worth recalling that simple replacement requires 2.1.
After the invasion of Ukraine, the issue acquired strategic importance for the Kremlin. Enormous battlefield losses and the outflow of young people have turned the old Soviet slogan "women will give birth to more" into a new political priority. Just recently, Putin once again stated that the "long-term task is to preserve and increase the population of Russia." Regional birth rates have also been included in assessments of governors' performance.
Senior Russian officials, including Federation Council Speaker Valentina Matviyenko, repeat the same message: "For successful economic and social development, to build our country and ensure security, there must be many more Russians. … A person's success should be measured not by how much money they earn or what car they drive, but by how many children their family has." Such statements are hardly isolated. Virtually every Russian state patriot periodically stresses the need to "have more children."
The "Carrot and Stick" of Family Values
Russia has sufficient resources to actively influence its demographic policy. The Kremlin has a broad set of tools for increasing birth rates — from financial incentives to outright restrictions.
There are plenty of "carrots": maternity capital, family mortgages, tax benefits, support for large families, and so on. The Kremlin is not sparing money in its effort to "produce" new soldiers. The "Family" national project is expected to spend 17.9 trillion rubles (about $200 billion at an exchange rate of roughly 90 rubles to the dollar) in 2025–2030, including 3.2 trillion rubles (about $36 billion) in 2026. Most of the program consists of various financial incentives and benefits for families, including subsidized mortgages and maternity capital.
However, the Russian authorities understand that this is not enough. The program's target is to raise the total fertility rate to 1.593 — still far below the 2.1 replacement level.
For those who are not tempted by financial incentives, the Russian authorities have a "stick": propaganda promoting childbirth and various restrictions. These include Putin's law banning the "promotion of refusing to have children," penalties for "inducement to abortion," a ban on private clinics performing abortions, and, more recently, discussions in the State Duma and the Russian Orthodox Church about requiring a husband's consent for a woman to have an abortion.
The state's "concern" for citizens' reproductive health sometimes reaches the absurd. Among the latest initiatives are referring women who do not plan to have children to psychologists, while men who are fond of saunas are to be sent for sperm tests.
No matter how comical these initiatives may look from the outside, the Kremlin is using them to relentlessly pursue its goal of overcoming the demographic crisis. At the same time, the initiatives are viewed critically — and sometimes even hostilely — by the population, creating yet another deep conflict within Russian society.
"Nravitsya, ne nravitsya — rozhay, moya krasavitsa" ("Like it or not — give birth, my beauty")*
At Join Ukraine, we analyzed discussions about childbirth in more than 700 Telegram and VKontakte communities across virtually all Russian regions. The scale of the sample allows us to identify both isolated bursts of discontent and clear broader social trends.
The greatest wave of outrage was triggered by announcements about payments to pregnant students and schoolgirls: 72% of reactions on Telegram were negative, while only 3% were positive. The "support" was perceived not as assistance to young women, but as an incentive for early pregnancy at the expense of education and professional development. Dissatisfied users asked: "When are they supposed to study?" Some even wondered: "Are women being pushed to have children instead of pursuing a career? And if the marriage doesn't work out, what happens next? Will the state take care of the children? Of course not."
The second-most negatively received issue was abortion restrictions. Users were particularly concerned about the proposal that a married woman should only be allowed to terminate a pregnancy with her husband's consent. For example, one post in a Rostov-based community received 1,473 negative reactions, while another similar post in Voronezh received 2,023. Commenters pointed to overcrowded orphanages and argued that banning abortions does not eliminate the reasons why women seek them.
Russians also strongly disliked the Russian Health Ministry's idea of encouraging women to become pregnant through psychologists. Posts about introducing mandatory consultations for women who say they do not plan to have children — in March 2026 — received tens of thousands of forwards and overwhelmingly negative reactions.
Purely economic programs did not generate much enthusiasm either. Posts about family mortgages were predominantly met with negativity. The main reason is that these mortgages are becoming increasingly inaccessible due to constantly changing terms and rising housing prices. Russians reacted relatively calmly to posts about maternity capital, although attempts by the authorities to restrict how the money can be used also faced sharp criticism.
"Sami rozhayte!" ("Have children yourselves!"): Why Russians Reject the Authorities' Demographic Initiatives
The main criticism of the Kremlin's demographic initiatives was rooted in distrust of the authorities and the conviction that they are hypocritical. This was reflected in the sarcastic slogan "Sami rozhayte!" — "have children yourselves!" This line of argument accounted for roughly a quarter of reasoned comments on Telegram and VKontakte.
Next came entirely practical arguments: poverty, high prices and unaffordable housing. Commenters also condemned the cynicism of calls to have more children while schools, maternity wards and clinics are systematically being closed and infrastructure remains underdeveloped.
A noticeable xenophobic strand was also present — an entirely predictable consequence of years of state propaganda that has taught Russians to blame migrants and other "outsiders." Nearly one in seven substantive comments on Telegram and VKontakte argued that childbirth benefits supposedly go to "the wrong people."
Direct references to state interference in private life were less common, but remained consistent. The war was mentioned even more cautiously: only 5.8% of Telegram comments and 7.5% of VKontakte comments directly linked calls to have more children with the need to replenish the army and compensate for Russia's losses in the so-called "special military operation."
However, given the censorship and repression prevailing in Russia, even these figures matter.
Women's rights were mentioned least often. One could joke that women's rights in Russia are so securely protected by the state that they are never actually issued to the women themselves. On a more serious note, the reason is the scale of "traditional values" propaganda and religious pressure, as well as the dominance of patriarchal ideas about the family, particularly outside cities of more than one million people.
The Kremlin's Demographic Plans — What Does This Mean for Ukraine?
Knowing your enemy means trying to stay at least one step ahead. That is why Russia's demographic policy has not only a social but also a direct security dimension for Ukraine. Behind campaigns to increase birth rates and promote large families lies the Kremlin's desire to preserve its human and mobilization resources for future wars. The Russian authorities themselves make no secret of the fact that they associate population size with military power, state strength and geopolitical status.
Even after the current war ends, Russia is likely to remain imperial and aggressive as long as it exists as a unified political system. Rebuilding its mobilization potential through new generations could eventually result in another war for Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's population is shrinking rapidly due to wartime casualties, migration and low birth rates. We have no time for complacency. We need to prepare now for the possibility of future confrontation — combining stronger defense with family support, the return of Ukrainian citizens, economic development and the creation of a country that people will not be afraid to tie their own future to.
The Kremlin is actively trying to address its demographic crisis. Yet it is proving more successful at deepening the conflict between the population and the state.
Our task is even harder. At the very least, we must avoid repeating Russia's mistakes in responding to demographic challenges.
- The phrase echoes Vladimir Putin's 2022 remark about the Minsk agreements, itself a paraphrase of a crude Russian rhyme.
All quotations from Russian officials and social media users are translated from Russian.
Liubov Tsybulska is an expert in strategic communications and a specialist on hybrid threats in Ukraine. She is the founder and current director of the NGO Join Ukraine

articles.title: The World Is Telling the Wrong Story About China
articles.body:
Compared with Donald Trump’s chaotic, divided, and violent America, China is a bastion of steady progress and serene order. This, at least, is the story that Beijing’s propagandists have been eager to spread. The Global Times, a Communist Party–run news outlet, proclaimed earlier this year that “the world’s peace and development increasingly rely on China’s stability.” The state news agency Xinhua chimed in that “in today’s uncertain world, China’s stability and predictability provide a rare and valuable anchor, which is set to benefit other countries.”
This message appears to be resonating around the world. A Pew Research Center survey of three dozen countries recently found that China is now seen more positively than the United States. Respondents expressed more confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping to “do the right thing” in world affairs than Trump.
China’s stability may appear desirable to a world in turmoil. But inside China, this “stability” looks a lot like policy paralysis, economic stagnation, and intensified political repression. What all the hand-wringing over China’s growing influence and surging exports fails to recognize is that the country is flatlining politically and economically. The evidence is in plain sight.
Policy makers around the world are understandably fixating on China’s abundant and cheap electric cars and competitive AI models, which present a serious threat to national industries. But these advances are one small part of a broader economy with pernicious and deep-rooted problems. The country’s property-market downturn, triggered by the 2021 meltdown of the real-estate developer Evergrande, has not hit bottom. Home prices continue to fall, eating away at the wealth of many middle-class households.
Trump’s war with Iran has pushed up oil prices, raising the cost of production for Chinese companies and ending three years of deflation. But the underlying problems of oversupply and weak demand remain entrenched. Youth unemployment, which emerged as a major social issue in 2023, has become chronic. The jobless rate among workers aged 16 to 24 stood at 18 percent last month.
These pressures have left Chinese consumers reluctant to spend. Retail sales grew a paltry 0.6 percent in July. Domestic sales of EVs have been falling. China’s economic problems have become so dire that some economists suspect that the official government statistics are overstating the country’s true performance. Although China’s economy has been growing a respectable 5 percent annually for the past three years, the research firm Rhodium Group estimates that China’s actual growth rate was probably near 2 percent in 2023 and closer to 3 percent over the past two years.
Any hope that China’s leaders will tackle these problems is almost certainly misplaced. Xi has stubbornly resisted the difficult and politically sensitive reforms necessary to fix the country’s economic model during his nearly 14 years in charge, and he is unlikely to change his approach anytime soon. He remains as myopically focused as ever on state-led programs to advance Chinese technology and industry, and particularly AI, and is apparently convinced that they will boost the entire economy. Perhaps this strategy will one day pay off, but the signs aren’t good. China’s debt has exploded on Xi’s watch—at three times the size of the economy, it surpasses even America’s debt burden. Growth in the second quarter of 2026 was the slowest since 2022, when China was still battling the coronavirus pandemic.
The Communist Party could theoretically change its leadership team at a major congress next year, but in the absence of any clear alternatives or successors, Xi is likely to secure yet another five-year term as general secretary. Xi’s ruthlessness in office has been marked by regular purges of possible rivals, generals, and members of other party factions. His latest victim appears to be Fang Xinghai, a former top securities regulator well-respected by international business leaders, against whom the party recently launched an investigation for unnamed disciplinary violations. With Fang’s fall, the government is sidelining yet another economic reformer with valuable expertise who might have helped fix the economy’s woes but whose market-oriented philosophy has fallen out of favor with a regime that prefers a top-down approach to national development.
Xi maintains social order through this never-ending malaise by controlling information and repressing alternative views. A sweeping new law took effect last month that mandates Mandarin as the primary language in education and orders parents to guide children to “love the Chinese Communist Party.” In prizing national unity over ethnic autonomy, this policy seems designed to force the country’s various ethnic minorities, including Uyghurs, Tibetans, and Mongolians, to assimilate into the majority Han Chinese culture. Even humor must follow the party line. Local authorities are reportedly investigating Guo Degang, a popular comedian who made the mistake of altering the lyrics of a patriotic song cherished by Communist cadres during a performance in the city of Wuhan last month.
Despite global surveys that report a growing fondness for China, the country’s “stability” comes at a steep cost to other countries. China may not be dropping bombs, but Beijing is arguably helping other countries drop theirs. By economically supporting Iran and Russia, Xi is essentially fighting proxy wars in both Europe and the Middle East.
In the absence of domestic demand, China’s subsidized and bloated manufacturing industries are exporting their problems and threatening the survival of competitors around the world. Given weak sales at home, Chinese automakers are shipping twice as much of their production overseas as they had a year ago. European Union officials are seeking greater powers and enhanced cooperation among its members to protect the continent’s industries from an onslaught of cheap Chinese imports, which have not only cost the region jobs but have run up a trade deficit with China topping $1 billion a day.
As Trump’s unpredictable and self-obsessed decision making saps America’s economic competitiveness and military might, China’s rise on the world stage is destined to continue, if only by default. But Xi’s insistence on preserving stability instead of addressing China’s serious structural problems threatens this ascent. Perhaps, then, the competition between China and the U.S. is less a contest for supremacy than a race to see which country hits bottom first.

“What’s Wrong With That Company?” Lavrov Defends Russia’s Alliance With Iran and North Korea
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov defended Moscow’s close ties with Iran and North Korea after being asked how the two countries had effectively become Russia’s main allies.

articles.title: ‘Every step towards disarmament matters,’ nuclear testing survivors warn
articles.body:
‘Every step towards disarmament matters,’ nuclear testing survivors warn
He was born without arms, a legacy of four decades of nuclear explosions at the Semipalatinsk test site in his native Kazakhstan.
Artist and anti-nuclear activist Karipbek Kuyukov walked through the halls of UN Headquarters in New York on Monday alongside diplomats, scientists and survivors, carrying a message he has spent his life delivering: no one should ever again suffer what his generation endured.
Mr. Kuyukov, who paints holding the brush with his lips and toes, was among the participants of a symbolic walk ahead of the General Assembly’s high-level meeting on the occasion of the International Day against Nuclear Tests, marked annually on 29 August.
The short procession, part of the #StepUp4Disarmament campaign, ended in front of a large photograph on display in the General Assembly building, depicting people demanding the closure of the Semipalatinsk site.
“I would like to tell our story, the story of Kazakhstan,” Mr. Kuyukov told UN News.
456 nuclear tests
Between 1949 and 1989, the Semipalatinsk site saw 456 nuclear tests. Hundreds of thousands of people living nearby were exposed to elevated levels of radiation, with consequences carried within families across generations.
“My parents were living witnesses of those tests, and as a result, I was born without arms,” Mr. Kuyukov said.
He was 20 years old when Kazakh poet Olzhas Suleimenov launched the Nevada-Semipalatinsk anti-nuclear movement.
‘Entire nation rose up’
“The entire nation rose up against this monster, against the Semipalatinsk polygon,” he recalled.
The movement reached far beyond Kazakhstan.
Mr. Kuyukov remembered standing at a protest alongside a chief of the Shoshone people, whose lands lay near the United States test site in Nevada, and joining peaceful rallies at the gates of Semipalatinsk with activists from French Polynesia, where France conducted tests at Mururoa Atoll, and from Japan.
Shuttered for good
On 29 August 1991, the Semipalatinsk site was shut down, a date the General Assembly later proclaimed, at Kazakhstan’s initiative, as the International Day against Nuclear Tests. This year marks 35 years since the closure.
“I can say with pride that my country, Kazakhstan, began its path to sovereignty precisely with that peaceful decision,” Mr. Kuyukov said. “I believe this is a great honour for us and can serve as a worthy example for other countries.”
Every step counts
Addressing participants of the walk, UN High Representative for Disarmament Affairs Izumi Nakamitsu said the silence that fell upon Semipalatinsk 35 years ago “did not happen by chance”.
“It was achieved through the determination of people, communities and leaders who rejected nuclear testing,” she said.
Kazakhstan’s Permanent Representative to the UN Kairat Umarov described the walk as “a very simple but very powerful way to remind us that every step towards disarmament matters”.
This year also marks the 30th anniversary of the opening for signature of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT). Robert Floyd, Executive Secretary of the CTBT Organization, told the young people taking part in the walk that disarmament is “a journey that works across generations”.
“The day will come when your generation will lead, will make the decisions, will be in the boardrooms, will be in the assembly halls,” he said. “And we will be cheering on your great steps forward.”
No one immune
Speaking later in the General Assembly, Ms. Nakamitsu warned that concerns about a possible resumption of nuclear explosive testing have re-emerged amid deep geopolitical tension.
She recalled the Secretary-General’s message: “the world must never witness another nuclear explosion.”
The President of the General Assembly, Annalena Baerbock, stressed that the consequences of nuclear explosions know no borders.
“In an interconnected world such as ours, there is no truly ‘remote region’ immune from the effects or dangers of nuclear testing,” she said.
Five generations of cancer
Among the speakers was Tina Cordova, a fourth-generation survivor of the 1945 Trinity test in New Mexico, who also joined the morning’s symbolic walk.
“We were the first people exposed to radiation anyplace in the world as ash fell from the sky in the days after the bomb,” she told the Assembly, describing five generations of cancer in her family. “We were never warned before or after of the danger, so we lived our lives off the land as we always did.”
She closed with an appeal to the delegates, saying that “after 81 years, it is time we set our families, our children and grandchildren free from nuclear threat.”
Message to the young
For Mr. Kuyukov, the fight is now about those who come next. Seeing young people join movements against nuclear weapons always reminds him that “in war, it is innocent children who suffer first.”
“The future is in their hands,” he said. “They, too, must secure a safe world for the next generation. We have experience and we can share it because we know how this is done.”
Asked what he would say to world leaders at a time when, in his words, the situation in the world has become dangerously tense, the artist called for reconciliation.
“To reach a new world – one of kindness, mercy and compassion – we need to let go of old grievances and past mistakes and leave them in history,” he stressed. “Now, we can only move forward together, showing the way to the new generation.”

articles.title: NATO's Arctic moves pose 'direct threat' to Russia, foreign minister Lavrov says
articles.body:
NATO's Arctic moves pose 'direct threat' to Russia, foreign minister Lavrov says
Aug 31 - Russia sees NATO activity in the Arctic as a direct security threat, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said in an article published on Monday, as the alliance members boost their presence in the region in the wake of Russia's war on Ukraine.
In February, NATO launched a mission called Arctic Sentry to bolster its presence in the far north, underscoring the alliance's increased focus on the Arctic amid tensions with Russia and U.S. President Donald Trump's push for the acquisition of Greenland.
Russia, which has a naval fleet including nuclear-armed submarines in the Arctic, sees the region as its sphere of interest where it also develops a shipping route to connect with the Asian nations.
Moscow has earlier protested the Arctic Sentry mission and in the article, Lavrov, President Vladimir Putin's long standing foreign minister, said Russia sees NATO military exercises in the region as 'aggressive'.
"Such military activity in the Far North poses direct threats to Russia's security. The risks of incidents that could trigger an armed confrontation, with potentially catastrophic consequences, are increasing," he said in the article published by the Russian foreign ministry.
Russia has the largest military presence and the most extensive military infrastructure in the Arctic and in recent years China has started to increase its activity in the mineral-rich area, mostly in partnership with Moscow.
Norway, a Russia's neighbour, this month expanded a recently created military brigade headquartered in the Arctic, the latest move by a NATO nation to boost its defence footprint in the wake of the Ukraine war which Russia started in 2022.
Moscow has previously dismissed allegations that it poses a threat to NATO. REUTERS

articles.title: Going visa-free with China, Ukraine peace: Putin meets with China, India leaders
articles.body:
BISHKEK, August 31. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin held meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday.
Putin proposed making the visa-free regime between Russia and China permanent.
At the meeting with the Russian leader, Modi suggested discussing Ukraine peace and many other issues, noting that India would continue to support all peace efforts on the Ukrainian track.
TASS has compiled the key statements from Putin’s meetings with the foreign leaders.
Extending visa-free travel between Russia, China
Russia is ready to work together with China to make the visa-free regime between the countries a permanent thing, if Beijing believes it to be prudent: "We are ready to work together to extend the visa-free regime on indefinitely if the Chinese side deems this possible and beneficial."
Putin also noted that the tourist flow between the countries increased by 43% in the first half of the year thanks to the visa·free regime.
Ukraine peace
Modi at his meeting with Putin proposed discussing, among other things, the Ukrainian settlement. He said that India supports any peaceful efforts to resolve the situation in Ukraine and will continue to do so: "You know that India supports all peaceful efforts in this area. We will continue to do so in the future."
Modi believes it's crucial that the fighting end in Ukraine.
India also advocates resolving all problems through peaceful means; "this is what all of humanity demands, and this is India’s message," Modi said.
Putin said that Russia is making efforts to end the Ukrainian conflict: "We are moving along this path."
Relations between Russia, India
Russian-Indian relations are strengthening, largely thanks to the "personal attention" that Modi pays to them, Putin noted: "I would also like to note with satisfaction that Russian·Indian relations continue to strengthen on the principles of a specially privileged strategic partnership. This is facilitated by your personal attention to the development of Russian·Indian relations and the fact that we have not only business relations but also very warm, personal, and friendly ties."
Modi said that he is sure that Putin’s visit to the BRICS summit in New Delhi in September would cement relations between the two countries. Moreover, cooperation between Russia and India is reaching new highs all the time: "We are extremely pleased that our cooperation is constantly reaching new frontiers and that we are working together for the benefit of the peoples of our countries."
Trade and economic cooperation is demonstrating positive trends: "In the first half of the current year, 2026, trade turnover has already increased by 2.6%," Putin said, adding that the growth of tourist exchanges between the two countries "reached 16% in 2025."
Putin said that India is also among the leaders by the number of students studying in Russia; according to his data, this figure has grown sevenfold over the past 10 years: "This is a good indicator: today it stands at almost 40,000 people." Cultural festivals, including those dedicated to Indian and Russian culture, are held regularly.
Cooperation between Russia, China
Cooperation between Russia and China is developing "in all areas, including the economic sphere," Putin noted: "We are implementing major projects in energy, industry, space, transport, and logistics."
The Russian leader noted that the growth in mutual supplies of agricultural products amounts to 34%: "Digital innovations, including those in artificial intelligence technologies, are opening up new vistas for the economic development of our countries."
"In the context of a complex geopolitical situation," the comprehensive partnership and strategic cooperation between Russia and China are "a model of interstate relations," Putin noted. "It is based on strong traditions of friendship, respect for sovereignty, equality, and mutual benefit."
The shared desire for peace and development remains unchanged, despite the growing uncertainty on the global stage, Xi Jinping said: Against the backdrop of unprecedented rapid changes in the past century, factors of uncertainty and unpredictability are growing noticeably, but the desire of the peoples of our planet’s countries for peace, development, cooperation, and mutual benefit remains unchanged. "Thanks to the joint efforts of both sides," Xi said, the foundation for the development of relations between China and Russia will become "even more solid.".

articles.title: Missile attack on Russia's Belgorod kills two, authorities say; hits Ozon facilities

Missile attack on Russia's Belgorod kills two, authorities say; hits Ozon facilities
Aug 31 - A missile attack killed two people and injured 16 in the city of Belgorod close to the Russian border with Ukraine, acting governor Alexander Shuvayev said on the Telegram messaging app.

Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022. The two regularly exchange attacks on each other's infrastructure, including ports, energy and logistic facilities but deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Reuters could not independently confirm the damage reports.

articles.title: Iran warns any hostile act will be met with decisive response
articles.body:
“If the enemies make a mistake, their snouts will definitely be rubbed in the dirt,” said Brigadier General Alireza Elhami, who leads Iran’s Joint Headquarters of Air Defense, on Monday, according to Press TV.

Iran quickly responded by targeting US assets in the region.

articles.title: Finland Cuts Russian War Criminal’s Sentence, Rules Facial Carving Did Not Cause Enough Suffering
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Finland Cuts Russian War Criminal’s Sentence, Rules Facial Carving Did Not Cause Enough Suffering
A Finnish appeals court has reduced the life sentence of Russian militant Voislav Torden, also known as Yan Petrovsky, to 12 years and six months after finding him guilty of three war crimes committed against Ukrainian soldiers in 2014.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Helsinki Court of Appeal partially overturned an earlier ruling that had sentenced Torden to life imprisonment for four war crimes, Finnish public broadcaster Yle reported on August 31.
One of the charges dismissed on appeal concerned a Rusich symbol carved into the cheek of a Ukrainian soldier with a sharp object. The court found that the wound was superficial, did not bleed, and did not cause sufficiently severe physical or psychological suffering to qualify as a war crime under the charge considered.
Torden served as deputy commander of the Russian paramilitary group Rusich. Much of the case focused on a September 5, 2014 ambush against Ukrainian troops from the Aidar Battalion in the Luhansk region.
Rusich fighters took part in the attack alongside the Batman Battalion and other Russian-backed formations, using a Ukrainian flag during the ambush. Twenty-two Ukrainian soldiers were killed and four were wounded.
According to Yle, the appeals court found that Torden fired a light machine gun at Ukrainian troops and was guilty of a war crime. However, judges said there was insufficient evidence to prove that he or two other Rusich members personally shot wounded Ukrainian soldiers.
The court also ruled that Torden did not bear command responsibility for the shootings, although it found him partially responsible for the deaths and injuries because of his role in the attack.
Other convictions were upheld. The court found that Torden photographed a Rusich commander posing beside the severely burned body of a dead Ukrainian soldier and later distributed the image on social media.
He was also convicted over online statements presenting it as Rusich policy not to take prisoners and to show no mercy.
In setting the 12.5-year sentence, the court considered Torden’s role as Rusich deputy commander, his participation in the deadly ambush, and the use of material from the attack for propaganda. He was also ordered to compensate wounded Ukrainian soldiers and relatives of those killed.
The Helsinki District Court had sentenced Torden to life imprisonment in March 2025. He appealed the verdict, seeking dismissal of the charges or a reduced sentence.
Torden was detained in Finland in 2023. Ukraine later requested his extradition, but Finland’s Supreme Court rejected the request, citing concerns over prison conditions in Ukraine. Rusich has fought alongside Russian forces in Ukraine and has been sanctioned internationally. Torden is also under European Union and US sanctions.
In a separate case, Ukrainian paratrooper Andrii from the 79th Air Assault Brigade told UNITED24 Media that a Russian surgeon burned the words “Glory to Russia” into his stomach with a medical cautery tool while he was held in Russian captivity. Andrii spent more than 14 months in captivity before returning to Ukraine in a May 2025 prisoner exchange.

articles.title: Colombia’s Abelardo de la Espriella says soldiers killed key dissident leader
articles.body:
Colombia’s president warns armed groups after military kills key dissident leader
President Abelardo de la Espriella vows hardline crackdown will continue, warning criminals who do not surrender will ‘end up in a body bag’
A prominent leader of the dissident factions of the defunct Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia who operated in a volatile area in the country’s southwest region was killed on Sunday during a military operation, said President Abelardo de la Espriella.
The president said the death of a man known as “Felipe” or “Arcadio” was a “crushing blow” to the dissident faction led by a man who goes by “Ivan Mordisco”.
De la Espriella posted a video on social media presumably showing a person in a body bag near a weapon and ammunition seized by authorities during the operation.
“We are closing the net on Mordisco and his networks,” warned the president, who announced that offensive operations against illegal armed groups would continue. “Any criminal who doesn’t surrender will end up in a body bag.”
He said “Felipe” was responsible for multiple attacks on police stations in Valle del Cauca, using explosives dropped from drones. He commanded a unit within the Jaime Martinez faction, part of the dissident groups of the defunct Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) that refused to join the government’s 2016 peace negotiations.
The leader also took part in planting explosives-laden gas cylinders on roads in Valle del Cauca, attacking a military unit, torching cars, engaging in extortion and committing other criminal acts, de la Espriella said.

articles.title: Russia is preparing to return a missile cruiser to service after nearly 30 years of repairs
articles.body:
Russia is preparing to return a missile cruiser to service after nearly 30 years of repairs
Kyiv • UNN
The nuclear-powered cruiser “Admiral Nakhimov” is completing trials after modernization. The ship will receive 80 missile launchers and cost more than 200 billion rubles.
Russia expects to return the nuclear-powered missile cruiser "Admiral Nakhimov," which has been undergoing repairs and modernization for nearly 30 years, to the fleet's active service. The ship is currently completing its shipyard and sea trials, Defense Express reports, according to UNN.
Details
By the end of the year, the Russians plan to conduct state trials of the ship, after which it could theoretically return to the Russian Navy.
In fact, the "Admiral Nakhimov" arrived for repairs as early as July 1997, although it was officially placed under repair in August 1999. The cruiser entered service in 1988.
The cruiser can carry up to 80 missiles
After modernization, the ship is to receive 80 launchers for Kalibr, Oniks, and Tsirkon missiles, which would make it one of the most heavily armed ships in the Russian fleet.
According to Russian estimates, the repairs and modernization have already cost more than 200 billion rubles, or approximately $2.3 billion. At the same time, the project's cost was previously estimated at roughly $5 billion.
Defense Express notes that the advisability of such expenditure on a single large ship raises questions, particularly due to the development of naval drones and other means of destruction that increase the vulnerability of large surface platforms.

articles.title: The US war with Iran has become a test for the SCO ahead of the Xi–Putin summit – Bloomberg
articles.body:
The US war with Iran has become a test for the SCO ahead of the Xi–Putin summit – Bloomberg
Kyiv • UNN
SCO leaders will meet in Kyrgyzstan amid US pressure on Iran. The organization is expected to provide Tehran with political, but not military, support.
The confrontation between the United States and Iran has become a serious test for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, which China and Russia have been expanding for years as a counterweight to Washington's influence. The leaders of the SCO countries will meet at a summit in Kyrgyzstan amid mounting U.S. pressure on Tehran, Bloomberg reports, UNN writes.
Details
Chinese President Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin will meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian for the first time since the beginning of the U.S. and Israeli war against Iran. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the leaders of the Central Asian states, Pakistan, and Belarus will also attend the summit.
Bloomberg notes that the SCO has expanded significantly in recent years, but contradictions among its members still prevent the organisation from turning its geopolitical ambitions into joint mechanisms for action.
The SCO is expected to offer Iran mostly symbolic support
According to the publication, the summit participants are likely to demonstrate political solidarity with Tehran; however, neither China nor Russia has so far shown readiness to provide Iran with military support, while economic assistance has remained limited.
An additional challenge has been the threat of new U.S. sanctions against Iran and the countries supporting it. Analysts believe that the situation could demonstrate the SCO's limited ability to protect even its own member states.
The SCO brings together China, Russia, India, Pakistan, Iran, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan. According to the World Bank, the organisation's countries account for more than 40% of the world's population and about a quarter of global GDP.

'Move from endless war to end of war'
Prime Minister Narendra Modi called for an end to prolonged conflicts, saying that every day spent in war pushes humanity backwards, while steps towards peace bring renewed hope."Every day spent in war sets humanity back, whereas every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm. We must move away from endless war and an end to the war. This is essential for the well-being of humanity," PM Modi said during his bilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Bishkek.Referring to the Ukraine conflict, PM Modi said India had consistently discussed the issue with Putin and remained committed to supporting peace efforts.
"We have consistently discussed the issue of Ukraine. When we met previously, you briefed me in detail on all aspects of the matter. As you know, India supports all efforts towards peace and will continue to do so," he said.Calling for an early peaceful settlement, PM Modi said, "A peaceful resolution to all issues at the earliest is the call of humanity, and this is India's message. The land of Gandhi and the land of Buddha share a single message- the path of peace. Today, I look forward to discussing these matters with you," he added.
PM Modi invites Putin for Brics Summit

It was their first bilateral meeting since the Iran-US conflict broke out in February."Calling for safeguarding the freedom of navigation and commerce, he (PM Modi) emphasised that civilians and civilian infrastructure, including commercial shipping and seafarers must not be harmed under any circumstances," MEA said.
During the meeting, PM Modi reiterated India's support for efforts to end the conflict and stressed the importance of freedom of navigation and protecting civilians and civil infrastructure in the region. "Met President Masoud Pezeshkian in Bishkek. Reiterated our commitment to strengthening India’s long standing friendship with Iran across diverse sectors," PM Modi said on social media.
"We want to expand and diversify our trade basket in the times to come. We had a discussion on the prevailing situation in the region. India will continue to support all efforts aimed at ensuring lasting peace," he said.

articles.title: Russia Floods Ukraine With Record Number of Jet-Powered Shaheds Straight From Factories

Russia Floods Ukraine With Record Number of Jet-Powered Shaheds Straight From Factories
Russia is dramatically increasing its use of jet-powered Shahed-type attack drones against Ukraine, launching more than 2,500 in August alone and sending newly produced UAVs into combat almost immediately after they leave the factory, Ukrainian presidential defense technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said.
According to Beskrestnov, Russia launched roughly 1,500 jet-powered Shaheds against Ukraine in July. By the end of August, that figure had already risen above 2,500—a jump of at least 67% in a single month.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Jet-powered Shaheds are being launched at Ukraine practically straight from the factory,” Beskrestnov said.
The numbers suggest Russia is not building up a substantial reserve of the faster drones before deploying them. Instead, newly manufactured aircraft appear to be moving rapidly from production into operational use against Ukraine.
Jet-powered Shahed variants pose a more difficult challenge for Ukrainian air defenses than their propeller-driven predecessors because their greater speed leaves defenders less time to detect, track and intercept them.
Beskrestnov has also drawn attention to an unusual flight pattern used by Russian drones heading toward Kyiv.
According to his observations, hundreds of the UAVs avoid taking the most direct route toward the Ukrainian capital and instead remain close to the Belarusian border for an extended portion of their flight.
He believes the route may be connected to communications equipment carried aboard the drones and their possible use of Belarusian civilian cellular infrastructure.
“I came to the conclusion that the LTE modems on the Shaheds, when flying along this route, are working with Belarusian mobile network base stations,” Beskrestnov said.
LTE modems can allow drones to exchange data through conventional cellular networks where coverage is available, potentially providing an additional communications or navigation channel.
Beskrestnov said the theory could explain why Russian drones approaching Kyiv repeatedly follow routes close to Belarus rather than simply flying directly toward their targets.
He considers another possible explanation—that the drones are being directly controlled through Belarus-based MESH communications nodes—less likely.
“The communications points operate much farther than just up to the border,” Beskrestnov said.
Earlier, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara stated that Ukraine has already field-tested four interceptor drone designs capable of taking down Russia’s new jet-powered Shahed-type drones and is now racing to refine the systems and manufacture them by the thousands.

Israeli fire kills five people in Gaza, medics say
CAIRO, Aug 31 - Israeli airstrikes killed at least five Palestinians in the Gaza Strip on Monday, health officials said.
Medics said two people were killed and several others wounded when one strike hit a crowd near the municipal public park in Gaza City, an area packed with displaced families.
Later on Monday, another Israeli airstrike hit a vehicle in the Tel Al-Hawa neighbourhood in western Gaza City, killing at least three people, medics added.

"I swear, we do not sleep from the sound of drones. You sleep scared of being hit," Abu Abdo added.
Hamas-led fighters killed 1,200 people during their cross-border attack into Israel on October 7, 2023, according to Israeli tallies. The Gaza health ministry says Israeli attacks have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in the enclave since then.
